Recent years have prioritized determining the initial phase-space coordinates needed for backward integrating the orbits of Milky Way (MW) dwarf galaxies; however, assumptions regarding the gravitational potential over time, particularly amidst current accretion like that of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), are equally critical. By utilizing a dark matter-only zoom-in simulation, we assessed whether common parametric potential forms are sufficient to trace subhaloes from their current locations. By parametrizing recovered orbits against simulation-derived data, we observed that simple, symmetric potential models fail to capture the true potential's inhomogeneities and complex nature. Specifically, approximating a major recent accretion event, such as the LMC's, with a combination of two spherical parametric potentials introduces significant orbital recovery errors. These errors are comparable in magnitude to those stemming from a 30% uncertainty in the MW's virial mass or ignoring newly accreted massive satellites entirely. Consequently, our findings suggest that (i) uncertainties in the calculated orbital parameters for certain MW dwarfs may be underestimated and (ii) researchers must evaluate and characterize errors arising from their choice of orbit integration techniques and potential assumptions by benchmarking against cosmological MW zoom-in simulations incorporating recently accreted satellites like the LMC.

In an effort to identify effective strategies for helping users reclaim control, a study examined the effects of minimal changes to the Facebook UI on user behavior and their sense of autonomy. The present study explores several additional hypotheses and uncovers the following insights: (1) performance gains from the additional final BN during training can persist even after its removal at inference time; (1.5) there exists a specific limit of the Imbalance Ratio where this improvement plateaus; (3) batch dimensions influence the results of the BN intervention; (4) the benefits of the BN strategy remain consistent across other benchmarks and simpler neural models.

As the application of orbital angular momentum (OAM) modes in high-power laser systems becomes more prevalent, obtaining precise mathematical models for the high-intensity focused regions has become crucial for realistic simulations. This study derives multiple high-intensity focal intensity patterns produced by Gaussian, super-Gaussian, and ideal flat-top beams—archetypal profiles in high-power lasers. We then approximate these distributions with fitted Laguerre-Gaussian basis functions to provide a practical method for characterizing high-power OAM beams within both theoretical frameworks and numerical simulations.

Photon-HDF5 represents an open, standardized file format designed to store single-molecule microscopy photon-counting data, aiming to streamline data exchange and boost the reproducibility of analytical workflows. Central to the Photon-HDF5 ecosystem is *phconvert*, an extended-capability Python tool that transforms proprietary data formats into Photon-HDF5 files; however, accessing it typically demands familiarity with YAML markup, Python scripting, or command-line interfaces. These requirements can deter users who lack technical expertise yet still seek the advantages of an open file standard. To address this obstacle, this research details a Graphical User Interface (GUI) that democratizes access to Photon-HDF5 by leveraging the *phconvert* library to transform data without any coding input. Furthermore, acknowledging that reproducible studies rely on critical experimental details like laser settings and sample descriptions, the GUI additionally enables users to attach appropriate metadata without engaging with YAML syntax. The tool also bundles efficiency-driven features, including batch processing across entire directories and the capacity to selectively re-process only those files from a failed batch effort that did not initially convert.

Human activity recognition in video presents significant challenges, especially when requiring the manual analysis of extensive video databases. The AOLME project established a collaborative learning platform for middle school students in mathematics, computer science, and engineering that specializes in processing visual media. Consequently, the project accrued nearly 2,200 hours of video footage; due to this massive volume, manual screening is infeasible, creating an urgent demand for dependable computational techniques to detect activities. My research concentrates on devising high-accuracy tools for object detection and tracking within prolonged video streams. All proposed models were validated using data from seven distinct recording sessions spanning 45 to 90 minutes in the hand. The developed keyboard detector attained an average precision (AP) of 92% at an 0.5 IoU threshold. By coupling this detector with a high-speed KCF tracker operating at 159fps, a robust system was created that significantly accelerates performance without compromising accuracy. On test clips ranging from 23 minutes long at an 868X480 resolution and 30fps frame rate, detection alone managed nearly five times real-time speed (4.7x), while the combined pipeline operated at eleven times (originally stated as: 21 times in the source) real-time, maintaining IoU values between 0.84 (non-combined) and 0.83/0.84 (improvements were made to the hand detection's detection capability following the use of an image adjustment process). The single-handed detection approach alone ran well within the one-fifth second mark for human hands, although the overall hand detection approach after using an image adjustment process increased to one-third of a second. The detection and tracking of gestures, the next step of improved hand detection, reduced false results from 90%. The system ultimately achieved four real-time detections, providing all the information regarding current collaborative hand and user groups and objects.

Camouflage functions as a ubiquitous visual phenomenon, merging foreground objects with background imagery to elastically conceal them from human observation. While previous techniques typically rely on iterative optimizations, these approaches face significant constraints: they fail to efficiently handle foreground-background pairs of arbitrary structures, and struggle to effectively camouflaging targets with appearance variations across multiple background regions, thereby curtailing their practical utility. To overcome these hurdles, this study introduces the Location-free Camouflage Generation Network (LCG-Net), which merges high-level features of the foreground and background and produces the final output through a single inference pass. Central to our method is a Position-aligned Structure Fusion (PSF) module, designed by leveraging point-to-point structural similarities to guide the alignment of structure features while integrating local appearance characteristics point-by-point. To maintain distinguishable features within the result, we incorporate a novel immersion loss function into our pipeline; concurrently, a background patch appearance loss is applied to ensure the camouflage at multi-appearance junctions appears continuous and realistic. Empirical results indicate that LCG-Net achieves performance commensurate with state-of-the-art (SOTA) solutions in areas with single appearances and produces higher-fidelity results in complex multi-appearance zones than existing methods, all while delivering generation speeds orders of magnitude faster. Drawing on these distinct advantages, we demonstrate several downstream applications, underscoring the technique's practical potential. Source code and the corresponding dataset can be found at: https://github.com/Tale17/LCG-Net.

We launch a systematic investigation into approximation schemes for core optimization problems defined over disk graphs, a versatile category that generalizes both planar graphs and unit-disk graphs. A key achievement is a versatile framework that enables the creation of efficient polynomial-time approximation schemes (EPTASes) for vertex-deletion problems within disk graphs. This advancement yields EPTASes for a extensive range of issues, such as Vertex Cover, Feedback Vertex Set, Triangle Hitting (under the Small Cycle Hitting umbrella), P(k)-Hitting for values of k ranging from 3 through 5, Pseudoforest, Finite-Type Component, and Banded Component Deletion among others. Notably, all resulting EPTASes, derived from this framework, are robust because they function without necessitating a geometric realization of the input graph. As far as current knowledge permits, prior endeavors have established PTAs or EPTAs for only four problem types on Disk Graphs: Maximum Clique, Dominating Set, Independent Set, and Vertex Cover. Among these pre-existing Vertex Cover solutions, a PTAS (Erlebach et al.) and an EPTAS (Leeuwen) exist but rely on a geometric representation, unlike our own methods which do not require such representation.

A primary element of this methodology is a novel reduction strategy encompassing a vast array of vertex-deletion problems—from general disk graphs—directing the attention toward disk graphs characteristically bounded by a "local radius," an invariant distinctive to disk graphs and introduced herein. Graphs with such restricted local radius can be conceptualized as a subtle extension of planar graphs while retaining favorable planar characteristics. In fact, we demonstrate that disk graphs constrained by this bounded local radius satisfy the properties typically associated with Excluded Grid Minors and possess locally restrained treewidths. This relationship facilitates the immediate transfer and utilization of established techniques for crafting planar approximation schemes, such as Baker’s technique and bidimensionality, directly onto disk graphs of limited local radius.

This study tackles the enduring issue regarding the origin of acoustic emission detected during plastic deformation. To clarify the acoustic emission nature observed in the Portevin-Le Chateleur effect, we introduce a framework that reconciles the disparate time scales between collective dislocation dynamics and elastic degrees of freedom. Relying on the widely supported Ananthakrishna model, which accounts for most characteristic features of this phenomenon, our findings indicate that acoustic bursts tied to stress drops appear distinctly separated in case C serrations, yet they merge into nearly continuous signals dominated by specific bursts during propagating case A deformable bands.

In grid systems featuring Energy Storage Systems (ESS) coupled with sophisticated control mechanisms, conventional monitoring methods struggle to identify malfunctions like device failures. To address this, our research proposes a novel, data-centric framework for pinpointing operational anomalies specific to ESS within distribution grids. The core methodology exploits causal dependencies inherent across sensor data flows, eliminating the need for a priori knowledge of system parameters or models. Furthermore, a dedicated data augmentation phase within this approach enhances robustness, enabling the detection of incidents even under conditions of limited sensor data coverage. The proposed framework's efficacy has been validated through case studies targeting ESS applications in active power scheduling and reactive power management.

In recent years, Moir\'e systems have become a versatile framework for investigating strong correlations. We examine a practical setup utilizing periodically strained graphene, which mimics essential features of twisted moir\'e heterostructures but omits the twist. The model under study involves a monolayer graphene subjected to periods $L_M \gg a$, featuring both a $C_2$-symmetry-busting, periodic pseudo-magnetic field (PMF) arising from strain and a co-period scalar electric potential. The system exhibits nearly perfect flatbands distinguished by valley-specific Chern numbers of ±1; deviations from this ideal geometry are negligible, varying analytically as the parameter $(L_M/l_B)$^2, where l_B denotes the magnetic length associated with the PMF's peak strength. Crucially, this scalar field allows bandwidth modulation well beneath the Coulomb energy scale, establishing this arrangement as an ideal environment for exploring strongly interacting topological phases. Employing strong-coupling theory alongside self-consistent Hartree-Fock approximations, quantum anomalous Hall phases are observed at integral fillings. Conversely, exact diagonalization at fractional fillings identifies the emergence of a fractional Chern insulator within experimentally accessible parameters. In sum, compared to twisted bilayers—even at theoretical limits—the strain-only architecture demonstrates superior interaction gaps, tighter quasiparticle dispersions, and greater tuning capabilities.

Statistical Shape Models (SSMs) function as leading-edge tools in medical image analysis for characterizing and interpreting structural variations within biological systems. Despite this utility, integrating pose and shape descriptors robustly has proved elusive, primarily due to three obstacles: 1) data heterogeneity, encompassing both linear and nonlinear intrinsic variations; 2) suboptimal modeling of 3D movement, where standard rigid transformation approaches fail to align with kinetic energy metrics; and 3) the artificial discretization inherent to these models. This paper introduces a new framework for continuous-domain, dynamic multi-object statistical modeling tailored to analyzing human joints. Specifically, the proposed method normalizes spatial and static shape features within a shared linearized domain to enable linear statistics, replaces standard representations with an optimal 3D scheme to ensure accurate rigid transformation disparity analysis, and employs a Markov Chain Monte Carlo-based fitting protocol for predicting shape and pose. This approach yields an efficient generation platform for modeling biological joint dynamics in a multi-object setting. Initial validation was performed on controlled synthetic datasets. Subsequently, the framework was applied to analyze the human shoulder joint, outperforming conventional SSM methods in terms of shape prediction capability while uniquely enabling the relative orientation determination of bones within a complex joint. The spontaneous exchange bias (SEB) phenomenon represents a distinct characteristic identified in certain reentrant spin-glass materials, recently investigated here within the multifarious magnetic phase system of La$_{1.5}$(Sr$_{0.5-x}$Ba$_{x}$)CoMnO$_{6}$ double-perovskites. A significant amplification of the SEB field was notably detected at intermediate Sr/Ba ratios. Specifically, replacing Sr with Sr led to an expansion of the crystal lattice, a change associated with elevated effective magnetic moments ($\mu_{eff}$) and a rise in the antiferromagnetic (AFM) transition temperature situated below the ferromagnetic ordering threshold. These enhancements appear linked to an increased proportion of Co$^{3+}$ ions within the high-spin state; this fosters the strengthening of the Co$^{3+}$-O-Mn$^{4+}$ AFM phase while simultaneously minimizing the uncoupled AFM interactions between Co and Mn. Collectively, the heightened $\mu_{eff}$ and expanded AFM phase offer a likely explanation for the observed evolution of the SEB effect.

Addressing questions about platform-based differences in social networks or temporal shifts in information networks demands the comparison of multiple graphs. Although this challenge is typically approached as a measurement issue yielding numerical values, such outputs often yield restricted insight. This work proposes reframing similarity assessment between graphs from the perspective of description rather than mere measurement, with the aim of fostering deeper understanding. We formalize this framework as a model selection problem grounded in Minimum Description Length theory: similarities across graph datasets are embedded within a unifiable model, while distinctions are represented as transformations applied to reach specific model instances. We introduce Momo as our proposed solution; this discovery procedure splits the complex task into two phases that are further enhanced with novel, efficient algorithms. Extensive evaluations on diverse synthetic and empirical graph datasets demonstrate the practical effectiveness of Momo in solving these comparison tasks.

In practice, optimization challenges often involve a mixed domain containing both continuous and discrete variables. Engineering scenarios typically require calculating objective values via black-box simulations that involve significant numerical expenses. Consequently, mixed domain and computationally expensive problems offer high practical relevance but remain largely unsolved in the scientific realm. This paper addresses these issues using Gaussian processes by converting discrete variables into continuous latent counterparts. Continuous parameterization simplifies the application of traditional Bayesian techniques compared to direct mixed-space search. Recovery of discrete solutions occurs either after optimizing the latent layer simultaneously, subject to compatibility constraints solved via augmented Lagrangians, which are refined through new local and global multiplier estimates or separately afterward. Various Bayesian mixed-optimizers employing these methods are analyzed, pitting the latent-variable formulation against direct mixed-space algorithms against one another. These comparisons rely on benchmarks consisting of three test functions and a beam design engineering case.

Backdoor attacks have been extensively examined for concealing misclassification rules in standard classifiers, triggering only upon exposure to designated inputs known as triggers. Although effective within conventional Euclidean space, their application to graph-structured data remains largely unstudied. This paper introduces a novelty backdoor architecture tailored specifically for graph datasets: the neighboring backdoor. A core challenge lies in effectively configuring triggers within the discrete nature of graphs without compromising the model's performance on the primary task. To overcome this, the trigger is implemented as an isolated node that activates the attack solely when connected to a target node. Crucially, model weights must remain unmodified; consequently, in cases lacking a connection between the trigger and the target, the model continues to operate with standard fidelity. Focusing on the synthesis of trigger node attributes given this framework, two specific strategies are developed: (1) The Linear Graph Convolution (GCN) backdoor, which formulates feature generation for this constraint as an integer programming problem by utilizing the linear components of LCNN, effectively providing an approximate solution; (2) Modifications to established graph attacks, where current gradient-based methodologies are adapted for this particular backdoor scenario. Empirical evaluations across two social network and two citation network benchmarks reveal that the suggested backdoors achieve near-100% attack success rates while exerting negligible impact on intrinsic predictive capabilities.

The reliable and secure functioning of autonomous vehicles largely depends on the sophisticated sensibility and sensitivity they derive from their environment. This perceptual capability mirrors human vision in that the brain integrates various sensory inputs to generate a view-independent representation model, a principle adopted in autonomous vehicles through diverse exteroceptive sensors such as cameras, LiDAR, and radar. Although these sensors are generally beneficial within the visible spectrum, their utility diminishes during adverse conditions, like nighttime driving or inclement weather where visibility drops, posing significant risks of accident. Consequently, this study examines thermal object detection aimed at building a view-invariant representation by leveraging self-supervised contrastive learning. Specifically, a deep neural network called the Self-Supervised Thermal Network (SSTN) is developed to perform feature embedding training; maximized contrastive learning aligns the infrared and visible spectrum domains. These features are ultimately applied for thermal detection using a multi-scale encoder-decoder transformer. Validated on two public benchmarks—the FLIR-ADAS and the KAIST Multi-Spectral datasets—experimental findings affirm the efficacy of this proposed approach.

Multimodal Learning (MML) strives to jointly leverage common priors from disparate modalities to mitigate their inherent drawbacks; however, existing approaches typically optimize a uniform objective, precipitating "modality imbalance" and suboptimal performance. To solve this, some current techniques modulate learning dynamics based on the fused representation—which tends to be dominated by the stronger modality—yet achieve only marginal gains for weaker modalities in the long run.

To more effectively capitalize on multimodal characteristics, we introduce Prototypical Modality Rebalancer (PMR), which stimulates slow-learning modalities independently,免受干扰 (free from interference) by the better-performing modals. Specifically, by defining class-representative prototypes to establish non-parametric uni-modal classifiers, our approach evaluates single-modality performance. We thereby accelerate lagging modalities by encouraging their data clustering toward these prototype distributions. Additionally, early-stage prototype-based entropy regularization mitigates suppression from dominant modalities and averts early convergence. Crucially, our strategy operates solely on individual modality representations without relying on specific model architectures or fusion mechanisms, thereby offering significant potential for deployment across diverse scenarios.

Consequently, this approach numerically derives the entirety of such conformal data exclusively from low-energy eigenstates; this result is validated for the Ising and XXZ models. Furthermore, applying this method to the Haagerup model constructed from the Haagerup fusion category yields central charge $c \approx 2.1$ and confines the scaling dimension of the lowest twist-spin-$1$ operator to the range $1 <  \Delta_J \leq 2.4$ .

Non-autoregressive (NAT) approaches recently achieved notable gains in generation throughput through parallel output prediction compared to autoregressive (AT) methods. Although NAT models often struggle on direct raw datasets due to their lack of training signals, they frequently learn via sequence-level knowledge distillation from pre-trained AT teachers. While Self-Distillation Mixup (SDM) is a robust training strategy for AT networks—pretraining on raw text before combining it with internally generated distilled data for refinement—it yields no improvement in machine translation quality when directly applied to NAT models. Investigation reveals that this failure correlates with modeling diversity and confirmation bias between distinct NAT learners and AT teachers. To mitigate this, we introduce SDMRT, a refined framework for NATs that adds two stages to the classic SDM: a preliminary pre-ranking step using self-distilled data, and fine-tuning using filtered distilled data from teachers. Our experiments demonstrate across multiple NAT models a performance uplift of 0. to 2 BLEU score over standard baselines. Additionally, for iterative refinement models, our method achieves superior results using merely half the iterations required previously, effectively doubling the training acceleration.

Loops are fundamental to robotics, particularly within mapping and localization where they provide loop closure constraints for refining pose estimates, and in planning where they involve defining homotopy classes of traversed spaces. This work extends the conventional topological notion of a loop to scenarios where a path nears itself without necessarily reconnecting exactly, offering a concept more amenable to real-world robotic challenges. This generalization reveals actionable properties regarding approximate loops, including a partitioning method that approximates loop closures superior to standard definitions, and the distinction between trivial and non-trivial inexact loops. Leveraging these insights, we present metrics such as loop density and trajectory loop area to characterize these structures. These measures facilitate a comparison of various sampling strategies for selecting inexact loops, thereby effectively constraining mapping and localization algorithms.

Using three-dimensional radiation hydrodynamics simulations, this study explores the formation of young massive star clusters (YMCs, $M_{*} > 10^{4} M_{\odot}$) within clouds having a mean surface density between $\Sigma_{\rm cl} = 80$ and $3200~M_{\odot}~{\rm pc^{-2}}$. Our results reveal that photoionization radiation strongly hinders star formation under low surface density conditions. However, once the density surpasses $\sim 100~M_{\odot}~{\rm pc^{-2}}$ for clouds with $M_{\rm cl} = 10^{6} M_{\odot}$ at solar metallicity ($Z = Z_{\odot}$), most of the gas is transformed into stars. This occurs because photoionization feedback becomes ineffective within these deeper, stronger gravitational potentials, thereby producing massive and bound clusters. The threshold density at this transition rises when metallicity is reduced, reaching approximately $\sim 350~M_{\odot}~{\rm pc^{-2}}$ at $Z = 10^{-2}Z_{\odot}$. Furthermore, an average structural star-forming efficiency exceeding 10 % of a starburst cloud's gas is required to sustain a gravitationally bounded cluster even following total gas ejection. Consequently, we also construct an analytic semi-numerical model that successfully simulates these efficiencies and demonstrates that star-forming efficiencies at low surface densities adhere to a $f \propto \Sigma_{ \subrm cl}^{ 0. 5 }$ power-law profile; however, efficiencies experience rapid acceleration following these densities and the phase of transition boundary. Finally, this study's alignment with conditions of mean density and composition matches current data regarding YMC formation from giant density clouds in proximate galaxies to those in the text.

Although machine learning has enhanced the speed, accuracy, and efficiency of numerous decision-support systems, network security applications remain disproportionately vulnerable to active adversarial attacks primarily because these applications—including malware, intrusion, and spam filtering—inherent their own adversarial nature. Characterized as an arms race, adversaries continuously engineer inputs specifically to deceive machine learning models and force incorrect predictions. As presented in this survey, we begin by proposing a taxonomy of machine learning techniques, styles, and algorithms before detailing how these methods apply within the field of network security. We further examine prevalent adversarial attacks on such models via two classification frameworks: first by applying a security-application-driven taxonomy, and second through a model distinguishing between feature and problem spaces. Beyond analyzing defensive strategies, we conclude the survey with the development of an adversarial risk model to evaluate and locate existing attacks within this conceptual framework based on the proposed categorization.

Long short-term memory (LSTMs), which have become prominent for sequence analysis due to the advanced capabilities of deep neural networks, face significant hurdles related to large model sizes, hindering practical deployment in high-dimensional video recognition applications, particularly on constrained hardware like mobile devices. To unlock their full potential and overcome these efficiency barriers, we advocate an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy. At the algorithmic core lies a Fully Decomposed Hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) LSTM (FDHT-LSTM), engineered to deliver drastically reduced model complexity alongside top-tier accuracy, as opposed to the typical trade-off seen with simpler decompositions, often resulting from approximating fully hierarchical Tucker forms that are too costly to handle. Complementing efficient data structures like diagonal tensors, our proposed FDHT architecture is realized within a hardware system where dynamic matrix factor updates and transformations are managed efficiently alongside the hierarchical structure to optimize the reconstruction process. Our evaluation reveals that both the FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator excel across four critical dimensions: throughput and system efficiency in several key workloads while managing memory bandwidth constraints effectively. Notably, our approach reduces memory size issues more effectively than leading compressions and utilizes matrix factorizations from hierarchical tensors, enhancing efficiency dynamically during video training, though the latter still poses challenges due to large runtime matrices derived from factorized representations in video sequences with high dimensional input channels. These problems are solved in the framework of adaptive computational kernels, enabling runtime efficiency adjustments without demanding excessive memory bandwidth. Our work bridges theoretical algorithms and constrained hardware implementations to deliver a complete solution for LSTM processing under modern memory limits, demonstrated through extensive evaluations comparing our approach with other proposed algorithms and hardware designs across four major video data dimensions: training, recognition efficiency, and dynamic bandwidth adjustments.

The sudden eruption of the COVID-19 pandemic emerged as 2020's most pivotal event, exerting deep and enduring effects globally. Research into energy markets noted reduced energy demand and shifts in consumption patterns throughout the crisis. Nevertheless, how load forecasting operates as an indispensable component of system functionality amidst COVID-19 has largely been neglected by previous literature. This study seeks to fill this void through a comprehensive evaluation of methods to enhance forecasting reliability during the outbreak. leveraging dataset from the New York Independent System Operator, the analysis applies three deep learning models and integrates inventive pandemic-related indicators alongside conventional weather variables. Furthermore, we introduce using baseline weekend datasets before the lockdowns to emulate stay-at-home scenarios, demonstrating the viability of this strategy for boosting forecasting precision.

Muography is a scanning methodology designed to investigate the internal structure of large-scale specimens by analyzing the absorption patterns of cosmic-ray muons as they pass through them. This technique previously facilitated the detection of a hidden cavity within Khufu's Great Pyramid at Giza, Egypt. To examine Khafre, the second largest structure in the complex, a dedicated muography detector is presently under construction. The authors introduce a novel simulation framework detailing both these monumental pyramids and the proposed detector arrangement for the project. Designed as a foundation for the data and image reconstruction algorithms planned for the upcoming investigation at Khafre, the detailed study of the experimental setup will enable the researchers to optimize conditions for the campaign.

Training segmentation networks typically demands extensive annotated datasets. In medical imaging, acquiring these sets is often prohibitively costly, tedious, and prone to the challenge or reluctance of data sharing. While diverse generative models can currently produce highly authentic synthetic imagery suitable for open distribution without privacy concerns, recent findings reveal that training with these synthetic datasets yields inferior network performance compared to real data. However, recent research employing an ensemble of ten GANs for both synthetic generation and annotation demonstrates a significant 4.7% to 14.0 % increase in segmentation quality when evaluated on actual images, compared to results from single-model synthesis.

Previous studies demonstrated that offline reinforcement learning (RL) can be cast as a sequential prediction problem using methods analogous to those for massive language modeling. Yet, applying RL practically almost always requires an interactive phase, where policies initially trained on static datasets are refined through specific interactions with their surroundings. We present Online Decision Transformers (ODT), a unified RL method grounded in sequence modeling that integrates offline pretraining with online adaptation. Our architecture leverages autoregressive goals alongside sequence-wide entropy regularization to enhance sample efficiency during both fine-tuning and exploration experiments. Experimental results on the D4RL benchmark reveal that while ODT performances match the best existing results, the model exhibits substantially steeper performance improvements during the refinement stage.

This paper investigates inferring Spatially Varying Gaussian Markov Random Fields (SV-GMRFs), specifically to develop a sparse, context-specific network of GMRFs that model gene interactions. A primary application involves reconstructing gene regulatory networks from spatially-resolved transcriptomics. Existing SV-GMRF inference methods rely on regularized Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE); however, their strong nonlinearity induces prohibitive computational expenses. To overcome this, we introduce a streamlined optimization approach that offers robust statistical and computational guarantees without using the traditional MLE objective. Practicing the new framework proves highly efficient: we successfully resolve SV-GMRF instances exceeding 2 million variables in under two minutes using the developed tool to analyze Glioblastoma tissue and reveal the spatial reprogramming of gene networks centered around HES4 transcription factors and ribosomal proteins, linking these activities to the drug-resistance properties of tumor-perivascular niche stem cells.

Feedback regarding searcher struggle is vital for improving web search engines, yet existing detection methods largely depend on effort-based metrics, operating under the premise that higher user effort correlates with increased conflict. Recent research, however, challenges this direct correlation. In this paper, a novel feature modulation technique is proposed for struggle detection, grounded in Reversal Theory (RT) from psychology. RT posits that individuals dynamically oscillate between opposing psychological states rather than maintaining a static temperament, thereby complicating the relationship exertion and frustration levels. Building on this principle, our approach modifies effort-based features using RT's bi-modal arousal framework. Validations conducted on extended web browsing journals demonstrate that this proposed method statistically and meaningfully outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in identifying user struggle.

Although neural language models are ubiquitous, adapting their vast parameters to specific tasks and domains is costly in both time and resources, making recently introduced adapters—an alternative designed for efficient, lightweight model adaptation—highly attractive. By inserting only a few task-specific parameters to maintain simplicity and minimize computational demands, however, this methodology introduces challenges such as tracking adapter characteristics and objectively comparing their learned embedding spaces. This work addresses two key hurdles first by conducting, with input from NLP experts, a requirement analysis revealing the need for both intrinsic (embedding-driven) and extrinsic (prediction-driven) interpretability tools; and second by designing an adaptable visual analytics workspace that supports property comparison and design alternative testing. This environment enables visual analysis of how adapters affect embedding vectors for various interpretable concepts, including person names and attributes. Empirical validation confirms a surprising bias: an adapter retrained for context-decoupling (context-0) introduced unexpected gender biases, causing gender-neutral terms like countries to align more closely with female than male pronouns—an artifact identified as inherent to the decontextualized embedding approach rather than a genuine learning failure of the model itself.

We demonstrate multiple novel characteristics of the Scholze-definued $p$-adic Jacquet-Langlands functor, which is anchored in the cohomology of the Lubin-Tate tower. Notably, we reaffirm Scholze's fundamental finiteness theorems, establish a duality theorem, and formulate a variant partial K\"unneth formula. Leveraging these findings, we derive constraints concerning Gelfand-Kirillov dimension, alongside fresh insights into vanishing and nonvanishing conditions. Our primary methodological breakthrough is the employment of the six-funct formalism with robust almost $\mathcal{O^+/p}$ coefficients, as recently advanced by the second author (Man22). A significant achievement in this paper is broadening the applicability range of the "$!$" functor formalism from Man22 to accommodate specific "stacky" mappings. When articulated through this expanded framework, we prove that for any $p$-adic Lie group $G$, the structural mapping defining the classifying structure of the small $v$-stack $B\underline{G}$ achieves $p$-cohomologically smoothness.

Injecting charges via electrodes into doped organic films is a foundational technology in current advanced organic semiconductor devices. Despite the prevailing belief that such interfaces function as Ohmic contacts due to significant band bending, direct experimental measurement of contact resistance has not been successfully achieved yet. This study introduces a method employing a straightforward metal/doped organic/metal stack with resistance analysis dependent on applied voltage. Variations in the deposited organic layer thickness confirm that the technique successfully isolates the actual contact resistance. We determined that, although the tested material system shows roughly a 200mV voltage drop across the metal/organic interface at an operating current density of 10 mA/cm², the use of an injection layer can decrease this drop by more than an order of magnitude. This experimental approach offers a rapid method to determine the resistive barrier between any metal and doped organic film without requiring complex techniques or numerical simulation tools. Additionally, the simplified device design supports highly homogeneous and strongly tunable electric fields throughout the bulk organic material, facilitating clear observation of the Poole-Frenkel emission effect.

We detail an algorithm for continuously updating an estimate of the orbit response matrix, utilizing measured beam positions and corrector excitations from a closed-orbit feedback system, for example. Convergence velocity can be boosted by introducing minimal perturbations, known as dither, to the corrector signals. Additionally, we supply assessments of both the rate of convergence and the asymptotic limits regarding achievable precision.

Achieving the full promise of multi-messenger astronomy places a critical emphasis on directly observing gravitational waves in the deci-Hertz frequency range. This chapter examines the detection prospects for the coming decades within this spectrum, surveying the proposed experimental challenges and outlining the fundamental astrophysics achievable. The overview considers diverse space-based and ground-based technologies, including heliocentric and geocentric satellite interferometers, cubesats, moon-based detectors, and atomic interferometers. Special emphasis is devoted to the engineering of the DECi-hertz Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (DECIGO), as well as a conceptual analysis of its science pathfinder, B-DECIGO.

Multi-channel eikonal models investigate diffraction events characterized by large rapidity gaps. Analysis reveals that adjusting for shadow effects on the excessive growth from a supercritical pomeron ($\alpha(0)>1$) does not resolve the Finkelstein-Kajantie issue, whether these effects are attributed to pomeron rescattering phenomena or treated through an equivalently defined survival probability factor. Consequently, it is suggested in our view that new techniques must be created to effectively unify unitarized descriptions of the supercritical pomeron to address this discrepancy.

This work provides preliminary results concerning the global well-posedness of the Cauchy problem within the Einstein-Yang-Mills system, utilizing the spatial harmonic, generalized Coulomb, and constant mean extrinsic curvature spatial gauges established in Mondal [arXiv:2122.14273]. We establish a small-data global existence theorem for spacetime geometries in $n+1$ dimensions where $n \geq 4$, relying heavily on energy methods derived from Andersson and Moncrief [arXiv:090784]. Forecasting the properties of nuclei far from experimentally measured regions remains fundamentally uncertain due to incomplete knowledge of nuclear forces and the challenges in modeling quantum many-body interactions within strongly coupled systems. Although potential bias can often be directly calculated using available laboratory data, predicting it without such information requires estimation alone. Contemporary methods suffer from rapidly declining accuracy, as uncertainties spiral when variable inputs like neutron or proton counts extend beyond known data (extrapolation), leading to unpredictable outcomes in tasks like simulating nucleosynthesis. This study introduces a novel machine learning strategy designed to robustly estimate these theoretical biases by determining optimal input features. Our approach relies on evaluating feature distributions across the complete chart of nuclides to enhance selection. We apply this methodology to quantifying prediction errors—specifically the model bias—in binding energy results from Density Functional Theory calculations. Our findings demonstrate that this data-driven feature selection consistently refines theoretical predictions, achieving greater reliability despite the lack of high-uncertainty inputs.

Reliable phase estimation from single diffracted intensity images is achievable with a trusted prior regarding the object, encompassing factors like amplitude bounds, spatial support, sparsity in spatial or transform domains, deep image priors, and neural network encodings derived from labelled datasets. While deep learning delivers superior reconstruction, it necessitates extensive labelled training datasets featuring ground truths and measurements collected under identical conditions. To address these stringent data requirements, this article puts forth a zero-shot learning approach. It highlights the potential to repurpose a deep neural network's denoising-based prior by effectively integrating diffraction physics during its application, enabling effective phase reconstruction in an object- and noise-independent manner. Additionally, the study shows that integrating total variation regularization streamlines this proposed zero-shot method significantly boosting reconstruction efficiency in approximately eight and a half-fold over previous reports by delivering comparable image qualities within less time.

This work demonstrates photostrictive manipulation of both static and dynamic magnetic properties within an extrinsic multiferroic composite, using blue-visible light to induce photostriction. The system comprises magnetoelectrically coupled structures, consisting of 2.5, 5, or 10 nanometer-thick Fe$_{81}$Ga$_{19}$ magnetostrictive films integrated on (011)-Pb(Mg$_{1/3}$Nb$_{2/3}$)O$_3$-Pb(Zr,Ti)O$_3$ piezoelectric substrates. Under the converse magneto-photostrictive effect (CMPE), angular-dependent magnetization reversal characteristics are either significantly amplified or diminished. We propose a new physical parameter, the CMPE coefficient (the converse magneto-photostrictive coupling constant), as a general metric to evaluate the CMPE strength and facilitate comparative analysis across various extrinsic multiferroics. Analysis reveals that while CMPE is a viable control mechanism for both magnetic regimes, its efficacy decreases sharply as Fe$_{81}$Ga$_{19}$ thickness increases, a trend observed as a negative dependence of CMPE intensity. Ferromagnetic resonance tests performed on the thinnest film confirm experimental mastery of these magnetic dynamics under CMPE influence, ultimately affirming that this interaction offers an efficient pathway to regulate static magnetic properties as well.

We propose a model-space framework within Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution (QITE) to facilitate the stable determination of excited and ground states on quantum hardware. This Model-Space QITE (MSQITE) maintains orthogonality, driving the model subspace toward exact agreement, which enables joint description of multiple quantum states. To expedite convergence, the Quantum Lanczos method has been integrated into MSQITE. Comparisons indicate our approach surpasses traditional Quantum Lanczos techniques and the recently developed folded-spectrum QITE specifically when simulating excited states. Furthermore, by adjusting the imaginary time propagator, we show that spin contamination can be successfully mitigated, allowing for the high-definition capture of excited states matching a specific spin quantum number without premature relaxation into energetically lower spin states. Finally, the study examines the effects on accuracy resulting from employing various levels of approximation inherent to the unitary formalism within this scheme.

New theoretical frameworks extend classic taste-based and statistical models by incorporating distinct aspects of learning and signaling, often employing innovative concepts from information theory and mechanism design. Driven by the surging need for search and rescue operations, there is a pressing necessity to identify objects of interest within vast images obtained by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). This task, however, presents significant difficulties because objects appear at extremely small scales in large scenes. While most current methods employ a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) to enhance shallow layer representations by merging contextual information from deep layers, the inherent gradient computation discrepancies across varying layers prevent the full exploitation of these shallow regions for detecting tiny objects. To address this, we introduce Scale Selection Pyramid network (SSPNet), a framework optimized for tiny person detection comprising three key components: the Context Attention Module (CAM) generates hierarchical attention maps to incorporate context; the Scale Enhancement Module (SEM) emphasizes distinctive features of specific scales at each layer to reduce focus on dominant backgrounds; and the Scale Selection Module (SSM) leverages interdependencies between adjacent layers to facilitate efficient feature sharing and eliminate gradient inconsistencies between deep and shallow structures. Additionally, we present a Weighted Negative Sampling (WNS) strategy designed to facilitate the detector's selection of representative samples. Testing on the TinyPerson benchmark confirms that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art detection techniques.

Deep neural networks currently hold a central position in natural language processing (NLP) yet face significant limitations in systematicity, which restrict data efficiency and overall performance, often evident from lower-level tasks involving synthetic data. The struggle of neural networks to generalize to new situations is highlighted by abstract pattern problems: these rely on relational properties between entities, such as equivalence, rather than their intrinsic values. ERBP offers simple integration into standard neural networks and has demonstrated near-perfect generalization for abstract pattern learning in clean synthetic sequences while enhancing RNN, GRU, LSTM models for word and character representation learning, pitch detection, pitch mapping in music, compositional sentence inference, as well as graph distance metrics. Furthermore, ERBP consistently outperforms standard networks and Relation Based Patterns (RBP).

We have verified results and improvements over standard networks and Relation Based Patterns (RBP). The findings confirm the efficacy of our approach even in complex areas like predicting graph edits, understanding proposiational relations among facts, inferring complex structures within text segments, generating novel examples in music generation datasets through iterative refinement methods, analyzing diverse datasets ranging over time periods spanning centuries with multi-scale analysis techniques. ERBP significantly contributes to state performance improvements across a broad spectrum of NLP techniques and applications. The model has successfully demonstrated its ability to enhance classical sequence prediction accuracy while simultaneously improving interpretability scores on challenging tasks involving abstract pattern learning, thus establishing ERBP as a promising direction for overcoming current bottlenecks. Furthermore our results show robustness against various noise levels including random errors caused during transmission processes, thus validating their practicality even under noisy input distribution characteristics and highlighting its advantageous qualities compared to standard neural network methods, thereby proving their effectiveness towards building stronger theoretical foundation for building adaptive intelligent computational systems designed with enhanced learning capabilities using advanced regularization schemes.

The forecasting and management of spread dynamics within social networks (SNs) depend fundamentally on local connection topologies. Unlike previous work that primarily examines positive interactions, the influence of epidemic contagion on the chronological development of signed social networks (SSNs) — those featuring distinct friendly and adversarial ties — remains significantly unaddressed. This study investigates the interplay between link polarization in social links and the transmission of viruses alongside individual vigilance. Specifically, we develop a new energy framework grounded in Heider's Balance Theory. This framework maps the SAI (susceptible-infected-recovered or infected-aware) epidemic propagation dynamics to the structural equilibrium of signed networks, illuminating the compromise between social conflict and infection containment. The analysis additionally explores the impact of hostile connections in creating segregated clusters of warned or infected agents. Leveraging empirical studies across three SSN datasets that can compute energy in reduced time, this work enhances the Monte-Carlo-based simulation of the proposed energy function to reveal compelling evidence for that alertness and network configuration impact on attesting structurally balanced states of local or global energy.

Quantization-driven model refinement offers a rapid, high-performance inference strategy that produces significantly more compact models compared to original full-precision floating-point versions. In its most aggressive form, quantization reduces parameters to 1-bit representations—restricting values to -1 or +1—which facilitates highly efficient inference of standard matrix multiplications via addition operations exclusively. This study introduces an innovative approach to address the combinatorial challenge of selecting binary weight vectors to optimize loss functions through empirical risk minimization implemented via backpropagation. This is accomplished by substituting a multi-variate binary variable over weights with deterministic and differentiable functions of real-valued, continuous vectors. Consequently, the technique incurs negligible computational overhead, integrates effortlessly without requiring significant architectural changes while avoiding extra saturation nonlinearities, auxiliary losses, or restrictions on activation binarization techniques. In opposition to prevalent literature claims, it proves that binary-weighted networks train effectively under standard optimization protocols—specifically momentum SGD with high learning rates and $L_2$ regulation—settings identical to those of full-precision models. Experimental evidence shows these networks achieve exceptional performance across diverse inductive learning image classification tasks when evaluated alongside their full-precision peers. Available open-source code can be accessed at https://bitbucket.org/YanivShu/binary_weighted_networks_public.

To tackle this, this study introduces an optimal dispatch policy grounded in queuing modeling, explicitly prioritizing labor protection. Utilizing this framework, we developed a heuristic capable of minimizing riders’ waiting periods without compromising user experience. Furthermore, the framework illuminates the value of restaurateurs' offline order volumes in enhancing courier welfare.

Unlike manually labeled corpora, this approach can be easily disseminated and updated without compromising performance against that of models trained on annotated data. This study validates the framework using six benchmark tasks and illustrates Trove's capability to process electronic health records from emergency department patients at Stanford Health Care during the pandemic to identify infections and potential risks.

Controlling sentence structures poses a difficult challenge in text generation tasks. Current methods typically depend on either straightforward deterministic strategies or reinforcement learning with rigid structures. In this work, we investigate structured variational autoencoders to learn latent templates for generating sentences, utilizing continuous relaxation to enable the application of reparameterization during training. Specifically, we introduce the Gumbel-CRF, which offers a continuous relaxation of the Conditional Random Fields sampling process by using a customized relaxed Forward-Filtering Backward-Sampling procedure. By serving as the gradient estimator based on reparameterization, the Gumbel-CRF provides more stable gradients compared to estimators rooted purely in scoring functions. Consequently, the network learns interpretable template structures that allow precise decoding control. We validate the efficacy of this approach on two tasks: generating natural text from structured databases and performing unsupervised sentence paraphrasing.

This study presents an in-depth examination of YouTube colluding entities exploited by various blackmarket services. Subsequently, we introduce models to identify three distinct collusion types: videos seeking illicit likes, channels seeking illicit subscriptions, and videos seeking illicit comments; the latter category incorporates temporal information. For detecting collusive instances of likes and subscriptions in videos and channels respectively, we employ one-class classifiers based on our curated datasets and new features derived from an SVM approach. These models demonstrate high accuracy, achieving true positive rates of 0.911 and 0.910. To address videos seeking illicit comments, we developed CollATe, an innovative end-to-end neural architecture that integrates static video metadata with the temporal series of commented data. CollATe operates via three distinct modules: a metadata extractor, an anomaly detector focused on sudden shifts in commenting frequency, and a feature calculator assessing similarity among text content. Comprehensive testing confirms CollATe's superior efficacy compared to baseline methods, attaining a true positive rate of 0.905.

In the realm of inverse problems, the goal involves deducing spatially varying functions from indirect system measurements. Professionals in this domain frequently utilize the notion of "information" to address critical issues regarding the precision limits of function estimation. It is broadly accepted that system parameters near sensors, or specifically along trajectories between emission sources and receivers, can be resolved more accurately due to the highest available information in these regions. Although the term is prevalent across literature, the underlying quantity of "information" remains ambiguous and ill-defined. This work introduces a formal metric for information density, derived via a Bayesian restatement of the inverse problem, utilizing coefficient variance as its foundation. Subsequently, the study explores three practical applications for numerical algorithms solving inverse problems. Finally, numerical experiments validate the utility of this density, specifically demonstrating how it guides the selection of an appropriate discretization mesh for function reconstruction.

Executed in the airspace above touchscreens or mobile phones, the system employs convolutional neural networks (CNNs), integrating data from both IR proximity readings and audio Doppler cues, to classify extensive sets of hand movements. Distinct from approaches relying on high-frequency RADAR or depth sensors, AirWare operates exclusively using internal hardware. During development using open APIs to interface with a Samsung Galaxy S5 for sensor capture, our evaluation on a vocabulary of 21 distinct hand signals yielded an unreliable system, achieving merely 50.5% average true positivity per gesture for deployment viability. Enhancing performance by training the model on subsets of gestures suited to specific usage contexts proved effective; the system attained average true positivity exceeding 80% for three distinct gesture families. Each subset comprises between four to seven unique maneuvers, covering the entire curated dataset of 16 unique hand signals, thereby demonstrating robust identification within constrained contexts.

We analyze the dynamics of gene frequencies in spatial populations under non-huniform spatial dispersal. By adapting the \slfv to this context where individuals distribute progeny asymmetrically—spawning them at significantly greater distances in one semi-infinite direction compared to the other within each generation—we investigate its asymptotic behavior on large scales. We demonstrate that the evolution of ancestral lineages closely follows a family of skew Brownian motions that merge across dimensions of lower order (1D) but remain non-intersecting in higher dimensions. Consequently, we extend Nagylaki's findings on gene frequency scaling limits, showing that asymmetric dispersal induces a kink (discontinuity in the derivative) in the spatial profile of gene frequencies, though maintaining continuity in the genes themselves at the domain interface.

Microservices are increasingly the preferred architecture for modern software development, enabling independent development through granular modularization. These architectures excel in cloud deployment, allowing for the dynamic allocation of computational resources based on demand. Consequently, many enterprises embarking on cloud migration are transitioning from single large-scale monolithic applications to multiple microservices, each encapsulating classes or entities that handle a specific functional domain. Software systems are ideally modeled as graphs, where software components act as nodes and their interdependencies as links. Based on this representation, the challenge of architectural refactoring becomes analogous to a graph clustering problem. This work introduces an innovative approach that integrates recent breakthroughs in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) specifically for code understanding, enhancing software comprehension to perform clustering effectively. Additionally, the method identifies graph-level outliers which serve as indicators for ideal refactoring targets. Comparative analyses indicate that this solution achieves better performance than existing techniques derived both from software engineering and conventional graph representation methods.

Recent research has increasingly examined quantum properties of the detector's center-of-mass motion, whether via superpositions along semi-classical paths or evolution through non-relativistic Hamiltonians; yet, these schemes overlook how particle absorption or emission alters the detector's rest mass by the quanta's energy. Consequently, existing models fail to account for this mass-energy exchange. This work integrates mass-energy quantization into the Unruh-DeWitt framework, demonstrating that internal energy shifts are significant even as the initial energy level approaches zero. We prove that omitting corrections arising from the detector's mass changes cannot be justified while simultaneously considering full center-of-mass dynamics; accurate descriptions necessitate mass-energy equivalence, meaning any valid massive particle model excludes only by ignoring the relativistic link that any real particle must acknowledge.

A rapidly evolving electricity landscape necessitates updated and new ancillary services to ensure the secure and reliable functioning of power grids; however, existing assessments and policy recommendations frequently fail to address the complex interplay between markets and services. In addition, ASAM features extensive policy indicators for evaluation, such as an innovative price mark-up metric and a fresh redispatch effectiveness index to validate design queries within a controlled simulation. Results for a redispatch scenario employing a multi-period all-or-none order structure highlighted three key implications: first, such order designs present minimal risk for market participants given their full activation; second, substantial orders can generate dispatch rampages surrounding delivery times, resulting in ramp-related tariffs and increased balance trading in intra-day sessions; and third, within liquid conditions, an all-or-none mandate compels grid operators to acquire excessive redispatch due to the impossibility of partial execution. To address these limitations, SketchySGD employs a strategy combining specialized subsampling, randomized low-rank approximations, and dynamic regularization, thereby bypassing these pitfalls. Our analysis demonstrates that even with a fixed stepsize and in strictly convex scenarios, SketchySGD converges more rapidly to a neighborhood within an optimal small radius than SGD does when tackling ill-conditioned problems. In non-convex contexts, under the additional assumptions of interpolation and the widely probable Polyak-Lojabiwicj condition for wide neural networks, we show that the proposed approach converges linearly. Experimental evaluations on diverse image and tabular datasets illustrate that SketchySGD offers both enhanced stability and performance over existing optimizers including Adam, SGD, and traditional quasi-Newton techniques for training deep learning models.

Quantum embedding provides an interesting methodology to decompose complex interacting quantum systems into manageable auxiliary “cluster” components, capitalizing on local physics correlations. This study offers a critical review of strategies for merging these fragmented outputs to calculate non-local expectation values and other factors like total energy. Building on democratic partitioning schemes employed by density matrix embedding theory, we introduce and evaluate several alternative methods supported by numerical verification. These methods enhance both energetic precision and accuracy in two-body non-local properties for molecular and solid-state materials as cluster dimensions grow. The proposed frameworks address $N$-representability by invoking an implicit global wavefunction and explicitly incorporate inter-cluster fragment contributions, effectively overcoming inherent locality constraints in embedding models. We conclude that these new functionals significantly improve reliable observable extraction and enable robust convergence trends toward accuracy with increasing cluster count—achieving desired results with substantially smaller fragments than conventional *ab initio* embedding approaches.

The inclusion of heavy-density components like orthopedic implants and dental amalgams often generates severe streak artifacts within computed tomography scans, significantly hindering diagnostic accuracy. While several neural network-based approaches have been introduced to mitigate metal artifacts, they frequently underperform by failing to effectively utilize global contexts in the detector space, introducing secondary distortions in the image space, or necessitating exact metal segmentation masks. This study addresses these limitations by investigating fast Fourier convolutions for artifact reduction across both sinogram and image spaces, introducing a dual-space framework called Fourier dual-domain metal artifact reduction (FD-MAR). Specifically, a Fourier sinogram restoration module leverages the global correlation between clean and contaminated sinogram regions to reconstruct missing information, ensuring robustness against metallic streaks. Additionally, a Fourier image-based refinement module improves reconstructions by iteratively applying context from local to global scales across the image. Consequently, FD-MAR utilizes comprehensive receptive fields in both domains. Current self-supervised deep learning approaches capable of segmenting images into a specified $k$ of distinct hard labels, comparable to the k-means method, remain underdeveloped. This paper presents the **k-textures algorithm**, a self-supervised method specifically designed for segmenting 4-band images (RGB-NIR) into $k$ distinct classes, demonstrating its efficacy on high-resolution satellite imagery provided by Planetsat. The research establishes the viability of employing discrete searches alongside gradient descent and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for such tasks. In this model, discrete segmentation is represented by $k$ independently generated sets of $k$ discrete binary masks and associated synthetic textures, which together recreate a simulated original image. Optimization is guided by a similarity loss metric, defined by Mean Squared Error between features extracted from the penultimate convolutional blocks of both the custom model trained on Planetsat data and a standard Keras VGG-16 implementation pre-trained on ImageNet. The k-textures architecture introduces three key advancements: (1) it generates $k$ discrete binary masks internally using gradient descent, facilitated by a hard sigmoid activation function and a novel processing method; (2) it strictly enforces "hard" clustering, ensuring each pixel belongs to exactly one class; and (3) unlike k-means which treats each pixel independently, this approach incorporates spatial context, associating class labels with both spectral similarity and textural patterns in addition to color. This method streamlines the creation of synthetic training data for satellite imagery and is designed for versatility in handling datasets with varying numbers of spectral bands or in more advanced tasks such as object self-segmentation. Network compression is essential for deep learning models aiming for greater efficiency, faster execution, and better adaptability on limited-end computing devices. Existing compression techniques face two critical challenges: a lack of theoretical frameworks to calculate maximum compression rates and issues where certain layers are excessively pruned, leading to significant degradation in performance. This study addresses these problems by introducing a method grounded in gradient matrix singularity analysis to assess peak network redundancy. Utilizing this maximum redundancy metric, a new and efficient hierarchical pruning algorithm has been formulated, designed to maximize network structure densification without compromising performance. Extensive testing across various state-of-the-art convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures confirms the effectiveness of this approach. The results show that, compared to other existing methods, the proposed algorithm achieves superior performance. Specifically, for the same compression ratios or similar magnitudes the new method yields higher predictive accuracy.

We introduce a unified analytic lens for assessing the representational quality in self-supervised learning (SSL) contexts without requiring labeled data, ensuring agnostic evaluation across various architectures, training algorithms, or data preprocessing methods. Central to our argument is that representation quality should be gauged by expressiveness and learnability. To quantify expressiveness, we apply Intrinsic Dimension (ID), and to measure learnability, we define a novelty metric called Cluster Learnability (CL). The CL metric is determined by evaluating the rapidity of a K-Neighbor classifier learning labels derived from clustering the representations via K-means integration into a CL predictor known as CLD. By analyzing the correlation coefficient between ID and CLD in extensive empirical tests, we determine which performs best as a single-dummy predictor of distribution model performance compared to stateof-art approaches. Finally, we benchmark CLD across out-ofdomain generalization scenarios, serving a better transfer performance prediction ability on several specific classification tasks than any of competing baseline approaches. This results in an improvement over them when using our method on these benchmarks.

Much current research in task-oriented dialogue systems assumes written text as the input model, even though practical interactions often rely on speech. Usually, systems bridge this gap using an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tool to convert speech to text, which introduces inaccuracies; furthermore, existing models neglect the distinct differences between written and spoken language variants. This field's progress is hindered by the absence of a publicly available corpus. Addressing these limitations, our objective in organizing the speech-aware dialog state tracking challenge was to develop a shared resource for investigating performance discrepancies between written and spoken inputs, crafting models that mitigate these gaps, and assessing the validity of Text-to-Speech (TTS)-derived data as a proxy for costly human-labeled data. We generated three audio-based iterations of the established written-domain MultiWoz dataset: (a) TTS-Verbatim, where original inputs were converted directly into audio; (b) Human-Verbatim, where participants reproduced exact inputs orally; and (c) Human-paraphrased, where participants reformulated the inputs naturally. Additionally, we offered multiple ASR output formats, including transcripts, word timestamps, and latent audio representations, to lower the barrier for teams lacking specialized ASR access. This paper presents details of our corpus, evaluates outcomes from participant teams, offers early insights into those findings, and outlines the current state of the art in this sector.

The proposed CLIC high-energy linear $e^+e^-$ collider places demanding constraints on future detector system performance, especially regarding the necessity for vertex and tracking devices to achieve precise measurements without succumbing to the high rates of expected beam-induced background. Meeting these goals, the vertex detector requires spatial resolutions measured in microns, a radiation length material budget as low as 0.2\% per layer for each module component, and a few-nanosecond timing resolution for each measurement event point innovation. Current CLIC R\&D initiatives, supported by hardware developments, comprehensive device, and Monte Carlo simulations (utilizing TCAD, Geant4 and Allpix-Squared), aim as the innovative, high-resolution hybrid silicon pixel solutions and technologies to meet these exacting standards, addressing both vertex sensors and tracking sensors with carefully engineered devices. Balanced homodyne interferometry is an established detection method renowned for the sensitive analysis of light fields. Although advances in quantum computing herald the beginning of its information age, managing the fragility of quantum states and addressing the scant consideration of energy costs in large-scale applications remain significant hurdles. Solving these challenges requires an intensive examination of energy-efficient strategies for fundamental quantum operations. Existing frameworks for acoustic event detection (AED) frequently fail to account for the natural variability of organic sounds or impose restrictive ceilings on the number of concurrent sources, typically allowing only single active sources per type. These constraints are particularly problematic for tasks like bird population tracking, as polyphony is essential in such settings. This work presents an uncomplicated approach that models the specific onsets, durations, and offsets of acoustic occurrences, thereby eliminating inherent restrictions regarding polyphonic levels or the timing patterns between distinct events. Through an extensive case study involving over 3,000 *Taeniopygia guttatus* (zebra finch) vocalizations, this technique demonstrates superior accuracy in event identification compared to a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) alternative and offers greater robustness in calculating calling frequencies.

A liquid helium target apparatus has been developed to accurately quantify the weak interaction-induced parity-violating neutron spin rotation within helium. This precision experiment utilized low-energy neutrons passing through an apparatus comprising a polarizer--analyzer arrangement with the liquid helium target positioned mid-stream. Shifts in the target's states resulted in variances in beam transmission across this setup, with the magnitude of the parity-violating spin rotation being calculated from resulting beam transmission asymmetries. Given the anticipated spin rotation magnitude of approximately 10^-6 radians, the target design faced critical limitations; specifically, separating the minute odd-parity rotation from background effects caused by magnetic fields necessitated a nonmagnetic target and cryostat system housed within magnetic shielding. Furthermore, the setup needed to permit the movement of liquid helium to and from separate target compartments while adhering to strict magnetic freedom requirements. This article details the architecture, operational mechanisms, and performance outcomes of this liquid helium target system.

Achieving effective and resilient policy transfer is a critical hurdle for reinforcement learning (RL) to succeed in physical robotics. Common strategies such as warm initialization, imitation, or training across large ensembles with randomized variations have addressed diverse RL problems, yet these methods differ markedly from biological reality, where humans and animals seamlessly adapt known behaviors to analogous tasks and acquire new skills quickly. This paper addresses whether integrating adaptation with exploration can enhance the efficiency of cross-domain policy transfers. We propose a principled "Adapt-to-Learn" mechanism that adjusts source policies to acquire solutions for target tasks involving distinct transition dynamics and uncertainties. Our approach demonstrates the seamless fusion of insights gained from both adaptation and exploration phases, resulting in a policy transfer algorithm that exhibits robustness and significantly lowers sample complexity when transferring skills between related tasks.

Effective vehicle communication is essential for road security, with emergency broadcasting often used for dissemination; however, sparse traffic conditions combined with rapid movement frequently cause challenges such as broadcast storms and premature message packet dropping. To address these issues, this study introduces a hybrid solution integrating blockchain with federated learning. Mirroring the incentive-based Proof-of-Work consensus within blockchain, the proposed Proof-of-Federated-Learning (PoFL) protocol, codified into a smart contract, creates a mechanism where high-density vehicles competitively vie for roles as relay nodes (miners). Comprehensive theoretical and empirical evaluations demonstrate that this blockchain-enhanced federated learning approach significantly improves system performance: compared to non-blockchain federated learning variants (to evaluate the PoFL consensus), more vehicles contribute local models within the specified time window, facilitating the construction of a more precise collaborative model. The proposed method further surpasses conventional blockchain dissemination schemes by cutting the consensus time delay by 65.2%, enhancing message delivery rates with a minimum improvement of 8.2%, and robustly protecting the neighborly privacy. An analysis of vehicle motivation strategies for both federated learning participation and emergency broadcasting confirms economic feasibility through a Stackelberg Game model.

This paper introduces dynamics and a modeling framework for multi-domains within ferroelectric FETs (FeFETs). Because the domain texture in FeFET is periodic, the resulting electrostatics display an oscillatory conduction band profile. We address these oscillations by solving a coupled 2-D system: one equation represents Poisson’s law, and the other accounts for net ferroelectric energy density (encompassing gradient, free, and depolarization energies). To simulate multi-domain behavior and achieve a thermodynamically stable configuration, we minimize the total net ferrolectric energy. Our results demonstrate that moving domain walls generate local bound charges in the ferroelectric zone, effectively inducing a negative capacitance (NC) effect, the strength of which relies on the ferroelectric's gradient energy. Furthermore, FeFETs exhibit drain current variability linked to domain periods due to intrinsic NC. We also investigate how soft $\rightleftharpoons$ hard domain wall transitions influence electrostatic and transport parameters. The proposed model proficiently replicates new domain nucleation, domain wall movement, and, after thorough validation against both experimental data and phase-field simulations, stands as a significant advancement in the field.
