We evaluated six theoretical frameworks—comprising one baryonic model, two dark matter variants, two Milgrom's Modified Gravity models with varying interpolation functions, and one Modified Gravity theory (MSTG)—against observational data from 18 galaxies, including nine high-surface and nine low-surface brightness galaxies. The dark matter simulations utilized either an NFW profile for halos and a modified density or an NFW profile paired with a spherical halo, or the NFW profile and the Core-modified profile. Evaluation criteria included Bayesian and Akihke Information Model Criteria, yet it emerged that no single model comprehensively accounts for the observed galaxy mass curves in all cases. While a pure baryonic approach successfully fit the largest number of galaxies, it relied on negligible contributions from dark matter; MOND achieved fitting quality for up to approximately 78% of the sample. The MSTG model performed best for just one case (11%), and the Core-modified profile managed only about half of the LSB samples. Additionally, NFW performed well in about a quarter of the HB samples. The findings, therefore, cast doubt upon the simplicity of using the NFW or Modified Core profiles alone to mimic the hypothetical halo densities required by cold or modified matter.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently demonstrated significant efficacy in recommender systems, predominantly by modeling collaborative relationships. However, complex scenarios in real-world data involve diverse entity relations, such as movies connected by shared actors or genres. Utilizing a unified graph for these heterogeneous relations often results in structural complexity that hinders processing. To tackle this limitation, our approach employs a step-by-step pre-training strategy based on divide-and-conquer principles. This involves decomposing the large graph into three specialized components: a user graph, an item graph, and an user-item interaction graph. By leveraging item attributes, we independently build multi-relational user and item sub-graphs from which node embeddings undergo pre-training. To facilitate this process, we introduced the Reinforced Attentive Multi-relational GNN (RAM-GNN) for generating robust initial embeddings. This method features a relation-level attentive layer that assesses relation significance, coupled with a Reinforced Neighbor Sampler (RNS). The RNS dynamically optimizes the filtration threshold for sampling top-k neighbors to mitigate over-smoothing during graph convolution. Recommendations are then generated after the aggregator GNN learns collaborative patterns from the interaction graph, initially leveraging the pre-trained embeddings. Empirical results confirm that RAM-GNN surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches regarding graph-based recommendation and multi-relational GNN performance.

The minimum detectable sample feature size in standard X-ray imaging systems is often limited by their spatial resolution. However, this constraint is surpassed utilizing the diffusive dark-field signal, arising from unresolved phase shifts or ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering caused by microscopic sample features that lie below the system's resolution limit. Accurately quantifying this dark-field signal offers valuable diagnostic tools for medical, security, and materials applications to determine microstructure dimensions or identify materials. While our recent work established a grid-based method for single-exposure characterization of dark-field signal based on scattering angle, this study specifically addresses quantifying the sample's microstructure size from the signal alone. To this end, we measured the dark-field response from polystyrene microspheres spanning five different diameters—1.0 $\mu$m to 10.8 $\mu$m (where $S$ denotes structure size)—to determine how scattering strength varies with these dimensions. Furthermore, we tested the feasibility of performing simple, single-exposure dark-field imaging using a derived equation for optimal detector-distance tailored to specific sample sizes and thicknesses; experimental results confirmed the validity of our calculation. Theoretical analysis indicates a square-root scaling where the dark-field scattering angle decreases proportionally to $1/\sqrt{S}$, a trend that aligns perfectly with our empirical findings.

The recently introduced identifiable variational autoencoder (iVAEs) framework offers a viable method for acquiring independent components (ICs). This approach relies on auxiliary covariates to establish an identifiable generation path ranging from covariates through ICs to observations, with a posterior network predicting ICs based on observed data and covariates. While the achievevable identifiability is attractive, we identify a flaw wherein iVAEs can yield locally optimal solutions in which the inferred latent components are conditionally independent of the observations relative to covariates—a condition termed the posterior collapse issue for iVAEs. Addressing this limitation, we present the covariate-informed iVAEs (CI-iVAEs), a novel strategy incorporating a mixture model within encoder and posterior distributions in the objective function. Consequently inhibits posterior collapse and generates latent representations rich in observational information. Beyond this, CI-iVAEs broaden the scope of iVE objective function into extensive subsets, allowing the selection of the optimal variant for achieving tighter variational evidence lower bounds. Validating our approach through simulations, and on benchmark images and memory tasks, we demonstrate its practical benefits.

**Background:** Advancements in droplet-based technologies have yielded vast quantities of single-cell RNA sequencing data. The main issues with existing methods are three-fold: (1) their performance quality requires further refinement. (2) Most existing frameworks necessitate pre-defining the number of clusters—a specific value that is often unknown prior to initialization. (3) There is an urgent need for improved algorithmic speed.

Therefore, we introduce the Para-DPMM model, utilizing "Split-Merge Sampling" on the Dirichlet Process Mixture Model. This model differs from traditional single-instance methods by conducting the Split-Merge operation directly at the cluster level. This strategic shift substantially enhances both the convergence rate and the overall optimality of results. Specifically designed for mass-data analysis on High-Performance Computing (HPC) clusters, our approach offers highly parallelizable capabilities. Benchmarking demonstrates that the Para-DPPMM model produces superior outcomes compared to currently prevalent clustering methods regarding accuracy and processing velocity.

The source codes required to run this model and perform similar analyses can be obtained from: https://github.com/tiehangd/Para_DPMM/tree/master/Para_DPMM_package.

This research introduces a pair of encoders and a decoder with diverse coding rates designed for the two-user Gaussian Multiple Access Channel (GMAC). By allowing identical codeword lengths but varying rates to match different channel conditions per user, this approach improves adaptivity. To realize practical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes suitable for rate-diverse channels, we present two new methods: row-extending (RE) and row-combining (RC). Our scheme also incorporates an iterative algorithm called joint rate-diverse message decoding for the user's messages (RDJD), which decodes all data streams simultaneously using a single parity-check matrix, bypassing the need to first recover linear combinations as required by traditional Compute-Foward (CFMA) and network-coded multiple access (NCMA) architectures. EXIT chart analysis and simulations demonstrate that, for the two-user GMAC, RDJD outperforms both NCMA and CFMA by up to 1.0 dB. Furthermore, optimal rate allocations are identified that maximize decoding performance based on specific channel conditions and target sum rates.

Specifically targeting lane changes, the study demonstrates how DMS utilizes this localized map to autonomously identify the most proximate neighbor in the lateral lane ahead and notify it via DIM regarding the HV's impending movement request. Autonomous Driving (AD) systems depend on artificial intelligence (AI) components to ensure safe and correct driving behavior; however, current AI algorithms are inherently susceptible to adversarial attacks. Yet, for AI-specific vulnerabilities to have a material impact at the system level, the attack must successfully traverse two non-trivial semantic channels: first, mapping the attacker's inputs at the system level to those understood by the AI component, and second, conveying the component-level attack effects back up to the overall system. In this paper, we distinguish the research domain of "semantic AI security" from general "AI security." While numerous studies addressing these semantic AI security challenges in AD have proliferated over the last five years, emerging data indicates that this trend is accelerating at an exponential rate. Specifically, we execute the inaugural systematization effort of this rapidly evolving semantic AI security landscape within the context of autonomous driving. Our analysis synthesizes 53 relevant papers, classifying them according to research aspects critical to security disciplines. Through quantitative comparisons both vertically among existing autonomous driving AI security efforts and horizontally across related security domains, we identify and summarize six significant scientific gaps. Leveraging these findings, we offer insights and strategic direction for the design level, as well as the overarching research goals, methodologies, and community standards. To mitigate the most critical gap concerning scientific methodology at its core, we have launched "PASS," an open-source, uniform, and extensible system-based evaluation infrastructure tailored for the semantic AI security research community within the autonomous driving field. Additionally, utilizing our prototype implementation, we demonstrate the functional capabilities and advantages of this type of evaluation platform by illustrating representative semantic AI security attacks against AD AI.

Machine learning in high-risk fields like healthcare encounters two primary obstacles: generalizing across varied data distributions despite restricted training datasets and preserving interpretability. For dataset instances belonging to distinct categories, the approach first computes probabilities regarding group membership (for example, stratifying medical patients by treatment facility or age). It subsequently applies these probabilities as weight factors within the FIGS framework, growing multiple trees where their collective outputs result in the final prediction. On pivotal clinical datasets, G-FIGS demonstrates state-of-the-art accuracy; for instance, while maintaining 92% sensitivity for detecting cervical spine injury, it boosts specificity by 10% compared to CART and 3% compared to standard FIGS, with even greater improvements observed as sensitivity requirements rise. By capping the rule count at sixteen instances, the final models retain interpretability while generating logic that aligns with medical expertise. All associated code, code, models, and data are publicly available on GitHub.

Intelligent, data-driven monitoring approaches offer significant promise for ensuring railway infrastructure remains safe and optimal despite rising demands for efficiency and reduced costs. Previous research indicates that track stiffness is a critical factor driving the evolution of track degradation and subsequent maintenance activities. Predicting porosity models from seismic data poses significant challenges due to limited resolution and high levels of noise. As an alternative solution, we have introduced a machine learning workflow designed to directly generate porosity models from raw seismic input using a ResUNet++ architecture. This process employs three distinct frequency bands derived from decomposed seismic data. Employed in a three-dimensional channelized reservoir for testing, the model achieved an R² coefficient exceeding 0.9 for both training and validation datasets. Furthermore, stress tests involving 5% signal noise added to the data demonstrated the workflow's ability to yield robust estimates under adverse conditions. Contrasting this approach are two additional experiments utilizing single-resolution seismic data via separate ResUNet++ models: one using the lowest resolution exhibited under-fitting behaviors, while the other with only the highest resolution showed over-fitting. These results underscore the critical importance of utilizing decomposed, multi-frequency seismic attributes for accurate porosity estimation.

High-order harmonic generation (HHG) within gases yields ultrafast, high-energy extreme ultraviolet (XUV) light, beneficial for fields like attosecond science and nano-imaging. This study reviews the HHG physics, specifically focusing on the macroscopic nonlinear interaction. By employing a combination of analytical formulas and numerical models, we examine how laser driving intensity and the physical properties of the gaseous medium—namely its pressure, length, position—collectively impact the conversion efficiency. Our findings demonstrate that highly efficient HHG can be maintained across wide variations in length and pressure provided they adhere to a specific hyperbolic relationship; however, the resulting radiation's temporal and spatial characteristics vary signiﬁcantly with different choices. These insights clarify the considerable versatility in gas chamber configurations necessary for efficient HHG while offering strategic guidance for the future development of high-flux XUV systems.

This approach generates the final selected feature subsets in significantly shorter durations. These results also indicate that the classifier yields better predictive accuracy than those relying only on these selected features or all available variables.

Human-computer interaction via head-mounted devices frequently relies on egocentric identification of finger gestures and fingerprints; this study presents a unified methodology to achieve both tasks. Our algorithm leverages a singular convolutional neural network to simultaneously predict the probabilities of finger classes and the respective locations of fingertip points within one forward pass rather than regressing positions directly from a fully connected layer; specifically, fingertip coordinates are generated via an FCN, with the ensemble average determining the final output. Employing a single-network framework significantly accelerates computational processing speeds, and experimental analysis confirms that our approach outperforms current techniques, such as Direct Regression and heatmap-based systems. Furthermore, the method's efficiency is demonstrated across diverse "in-the-wild" scenarios and practical use cases involving virtual reality application.

As energy consumption grows into a major concern for large-scale supercomputing, data centers face severe constraints due to costs when upgrading their power infrastructure to support higher computing capacity. At Los Alamos National Laboratory, future supercomputers are projected to face power limits rather than financial ones; acquiring new nodes becomes cheaper than overhauling the facility's power capacity. Consequently, upcoming high-performance machines may technically exceed their available power supply, necessitating strict power capping per node or job to keep total system draw within limits. This report introduces a statistically robust framework that predicts job-level power requirements with uncertainty quantification to determine optimal capping strategies. By employing hierarchical Bayesian models—integrating Hidden Markov Models and Dirichlet processes—the authors model power consumption at both the job and machine levels. Finally, they demonstrate how this approach can integrate into power management schemes to minimize the negative impact of capping on user workloads.

Efficient exploration poses a persistent challenge in reinforcement learning, particularly in environments with scarce rewards. Developmental systems can address this constraint by integrating information from demonstrations and self-exploration; however, current methods often fail in real-world robotics because they are constrained to Markov decision process (MDP) environments, lacking adaptability for partially observable scenarios where past history informs decision making. By extending the concept of demonstrating replay for memory-dependent control tasks, this paper introduces a new algorithm named Recurrent Actor-Critic with Demonstration and Experience Replay (READER). Experimental validation across multiple tasks critical for continuous memory handling demonstrates that READER significantly reduces the number of environmental interactions required, even with limited demonstration data, and outperforms baseline reinforcement learning approaches designed specifically for demonstration-based, memory-driven control in terms of sample efficiency and overall learning capability.

The output—artificial sequences that adhere strictly to graphotactic rules—is intended to serve as an aid for modeling morphological inflections in under-resourced language settings.

This paper introduces a new Bayesian online prediction algorithm for ad hoc teamwork under partial observability (ATPO). Unlike earlier approaches assuming complete environmental observability, ATPO allows for on-the-fly cooperation with unidentified teammates performing unknown tasks without requiring a pre-established coordination protocol. By leveraging the agent's local observations, ATPO distinguishes between ongoing unknown tasks. Notably, our approach does not require visibility of the teammates' actions or access to an environment reward signal. We assessed ATPO's performance across three domains: two variants of the Pursuit environment modified for partial observability, as well as Overcooked. Our results demonstrate that ATPO effectively and robustly determines the correct task from a broad library of candidates. Furthermore, it efficiently solves these tasks within near-optimal frames and successfully scales when problem sizes increase significantly in ad hoc teaming contexts.

Blood oxygen leveldependent (BOLD) MRI combined with maternal hyperoxia serves as a valuable method for evaluating oxygen transport and placental function. Analyses require tracking signal fluctuations across a time series, necessitating the segmentation of the placenta in every frame. Because BOLD time sequences contain extensive data volumes and existing methods depend on registration against manually annotated templates to align them, challenges often arise due to the placenta undergoing significant distortations caused by fetal movement, maternal activity, and contractions, frequently leading to the exclusion of many time points. To address this, we introduce an automated machine learning system based on a U-Net architecture, explicitly trained to segment the placenta in BOLD time-series data without relying on registration fails. Utilizing a boundary-weighted loss function, our approach enhances shape accuracy in capturing placental contours. The model has been developed and validated on a cohort of 91 subjects comprising individuals with both normal fetal development and those affected by fetal growth restriction and maternal obesity (high BMI). This method achieved a Dice similarity score of $0.83 \pm 0.04$ when compared to ground truth labels, demonstrating consistent performance during segments in both regular (normoxic) and oxygen-rich (hyperoxic) periods of the scan. The source code and pre-trained model are publicly accessible at https://github.com/mabulnaga/automatic-placenta-segmentation.

Determining whether a biological population will endure or face extinction is a central concern in ecology. We use mathematical methods to study individual behaviors in a way that forecasts ultimate survival. A frequently used framework for population dynamics is the exclusion-type random walk on a lattice, which integrates processes like movement and demographic changes while respecting finite system constraints. Simulating enough iterations of such random walk models to reveal average population trends requires significant computational effort; thus, continuum approximations are standard practice. However, traditional continuum approaches usually fail to reliably estimate extinction rates differently from the discrete case described by these models. Our work introduces a state space diffusion approximation, a novel continuum method specifically designed to incorporate explicit extinction dynamics. Our results show this new approximation reliably reproduces behaviors observed in random walk computations and yields insights unavailable from conventional models. We also investigate how parameters such as grid size and initial individual count influence long-term dynamics, illustrating how using this approximate framework substantially reduces simulation run times for long-term projections on grids compared to discrete approaches like the original.

This paper presents a method to address the difficulty of prostate segmentation on a rugged trans-rectal ultrasound (TRUS) image set by leveraging a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and statistical shape models (SSMs). Since TRUS is widely utilized for various prostate-guided interventions, achieving rapid and precise organ delineation is vital for treatment planning and fusing data with other imaging modalties, particularly Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). Nevertheless, TRUS imaging exhibits weak soft-tissue differentiation and a low signal-to-noise ratio, making segmentation difficult and susceptible to variable human observation; this challenge is most pronounced at the base and apex, where defining the glandular border is particularly ambiguous. We integrate this MRI-derived shape prior with a prostate regional tissue probability map generated by a convolutional neural network to achieve robust segmentation.

Penning traps, capable of trapping vast clouds of ions to create two- and three-dimensional crystal arrays offering scalable routes for trapped-ion quantum computing, are frequently paired like RF Paul traps with lasers to facilitate multi-qubit entanglement in quantum simulations and applications. A dominant source of error during these operations remains off-resonant spontaneous emission. While clock qubits serve as the standard foundation in many quantum simulators and computers, high magnetic field environments characteristic of Penning traps necessitates reliance on Zeeman qubits, requiring rigorous theoretical modeling to account associated coherent effects with decoherence. Focusing on such high magnetic field regimes, we conduct a comprehensive theoretical analysis of spontaneous emission impacts on quantum gates operated within the Penning trap. We analyze this effect across light-shift gates and the celebrated Mølmer-Sorensen gates and compare the resulting decoherence errors under the best conditions. A comparative study also varies experimental parameters including polarization and the detuning across the distinct gate types, evaluating the feasibility and performance of the optimal settings, which can achieve essentially similar efficiencies across the board for spontaneous emission. We contrast the maximum fidelities accessible at high magnetic field strengths versus those achieved by the best recent non-Penning (low field) two-qubit gates and show that spontaneous emission accounts for roughly a ten-fold degradation in fidelity for current implementations of the NIST Penning trap system. While identifying existing configuration defects, we propose several alternative configurations that bring their accuracy closer to, and potentially within the limits of today's advanced low-field two-qubit gates to validate these options.

Lung cancer represents the primary global cause of cancer death and includes various histopathological subtypes, with Lung Adenocarcinoma (LUAD) currently being the most common. While standard practice relies on surgical resection to assess the invasiveness of these malignancies, this intervention is often not timed effectively for immediate cancer management. An alternative methodology involves examining chest Computed Tomography (CT) scans; however, relying on radiologists for manual assessment introduces subjectivity and can lead to reduced precision. This study proposes the development of a novel "CAE-Transformer" architecture, designed for the efficient classification of lung cancer using entire CT images without the need for detailed nodule annotations. Functioning with minimal supervision and effective training even on limited datasets, the model employs an encoder layer to retrieve salient features from individual CT slices, which are subsequently processed by adapted transformer components to model global relationships between slices and deliver disease classification. Validation using a unique collection of 114 pathologically confirmed Sub-solid Nodules (SSN) shows that the CAE-Transformer exceeds the performance of competing models. Across 10-fold cross-validations, the proposed approach reached an 87.73% classification accuracy, with a sensitivity of 88.67%, a specificity of 86.33%, and an 0.913 AUC.

Investigating how groups, such as fish or humans, move together has long been a key area of research. However, real-world challenges like occlusions and changing lighting conditions can cause existing tracking systems to drop agents, leading to broken trajectory records. In this work, we introduce an upgraded deep autoencoder (DA) trained exclusively on complete portion of trajectories. Specifically, the loss function utilizes the element-by-element product of a binary mask indicating fully observed data and the absolute difference between the model's output and the target. Leveraging the inherent low-rank structure of collective motion—driven by inter-agent interactions and mutual dependencies as a foundational pattern, the new method termed Hadamard deep autoencoder (HDA) encodes information during training to facilitate trajectory repair. Finally, the efficacy of this proposed approach is benchmarked against a standard low-rank matrix completion strategy specifically for reconstructing fragmented trajectories.

The forthcoming space-based detector LISA will observe compact binaries featuring paired neutron stars. Combining LISA data with electromagnetic follow-ups could significantly advance our knowledge of neutron star physics and the evolutionary paths of such binaries. This study evaluates how variations in Milky Way structural models influence projections regarding the detectability, characterization, and resolution of double neutron star systems by LISA. We find that the spatial and gravitational-wave frequency distributions of the event populations are remarkably robust and largely unaffected by specific galactic model choices, unlike they often are by statistical fluctuation in small samples. This suggests that the computationally expensive process of tracing Galactic orbits precisely for binaries is extraneous. Conversely, binary eccentricity distributions exhibit a high sensitivity to adopted models of local star-formation history. specifically, any binaries expected to have measurable eccentricities greater than 0.1 within LISA's observational parameters are found to be younger than 100 Myr. We caution that comparative predictive models for LISA results require consistent star-formation history inputs and that the Galaxy's specific star-formation history must be incorporated into the actual analysis of detected observations.

Mobility data volumes fluctuate significantly between regions, which often impairs the effectiveness of spatial recommender systems that depend exclusively on data from specific locales. This paper introduces REFORMD, an innovative transfer learning architecture designed to enable accurate, continuous-time location prediction in areas suffering from sparse check-ins. Our approach models user-unique check-in streams within a region using a marked temporal point process (MTPP) augmented with normalizing flows to capture inter-check-in durations and geo-patterns subsequently. We leverage spatial-temporal flow parameters derived from source regions with abundant data as priors to forecast the subsequent visit time in destinations with limited datasets. To accommodate shifting regional behaviors, REFORMD upgrades the joint MTPP and spatial-temporal flow parameters by optimizing their collective likelihood with a triple-streaming mechanism predicting future category, exact timing, and travel displacement, all in support of localization. Thorough evaluations across diverse user datasets in the US and Japanese landscapes demonstrate that our system markedly outdistances existing state-of-the-art techniques for modeling continuous temporal sequences. Accurate estimation of post-click Conversion Rate (CVR) rates is vital for e-commerce, yet practical CVR prediction often faces three significant hurdles: data sparsity, where conversion data is extremely limited compared to impression counts; sample selection bias, occurring when models trained on clicked impressions are evaluated on the full space of all impressions; and delayed feedback, where the lag in observing conversions after clicks leads to imbalanced, often flawed training data (false negatives). While previous research primarily addresses single or dual issues in isolation, our study introduces a neural framework called ESDF to handle all three challenges concurrently. Distinct from existing methods, our approach views CVR prediction across the entire impression space and effectively integrates user sequential behavioral patterns with delay factors. To mitigate selection bias and alleviate sparsity caused by the scarcity of click data, the proposed method applies the user action sequences over the entire impression domain and jointly optimizes CTR and CVR networks via shared embeddings. Moreover, in contrast to conventional techniques that rely on assumptions about how conversion delays are distributed, our method discretizes delay times into daily intervals and applies a deep neural survival analysis approach to model delay-related probabilities. This strategy offers a more robust solution suitable for real-world industrial applications. Comprehensive experiments were conducted to validate the approach, making ESDF, to our knowledge, the first unified method to jointly resolve these three intertwined difficulties in e-commerce CVR prediction effectively.

Object counting is dedicated to estimating the quantities of items within images, with dominant techniques currently targeting single classes while achieving significant successes. Yet, real-world imagery often encompasses diverse object categories, making Multi-class Object Counting a task capable of broadening the domain's applicability. While existing multi-target detection methods handle counting in specific scenarios, they rely on bounding-box annotations, which prove significantly harder to acquire than the point-level marks standard in most object counting problems. In this study, we introduce a straightforward and effective counting network designed for use with sparse point-level data. We modify conventional approaches by adjusting the output channel count from unitary to categorical levels. Additionally, because all classes in this shared architecture draw from the same feature extractor, their features may interfere; consequently, we develop a multi-mask mechanism to inhibit detrimental interactions between object instances. Subsequent testing on demanding benchmarks demonstrates that our method delivers state-of-the-art performance.

This study focuses on reconstructing a high-rank matrix with partially observed entries, where its columns follow nonlinear structures including subspace unions, algebraic varieties, or cluster-based grouping. The recovery task is framed as rank minimization of a nonlinear transformed version of the original matrix, further approximated via a constrained, non-convex optimization problem on the Grassmann manifold. Two families of algorithms are introduced: one based on Riemannian optimization and another employing alternating minimization, each offering first- and second-order implementations. Theoretically supported, we provide convergence and computational complexity bounds specifically for the alternating approach. Furthermore, by utilizing the Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz property, we demonstrate that this alternating algorithm converges uniquely. Extensive experiments validate these methods for subspace union recovery and clustering across both entry-wise and dense Gaussian sampling schemes, resulting in competitive performance and high recovery accuracy, particularly with the Riemannian second-order strategy.

Leading firms, including Meta and Google, have launched "data-for-good" initiatives that sanitize and publicly release aggregated location data to benefit transportation, public health efforts like COVID-19 tracking, and urban development. While differential privacy serves as the primary framework for protecting the identities of data contributors, current methods under user-level privacy—such as those where each individual submits multiple location reports—are limited in preserving data utility. Consequently, these major releases compensate using extremely high privacy budgets (e.g., $\epsilon=10-100)$, which undermines actual data privacy. We present a novel method to publish spatio-temporal data both securely and accurately by leveraging the denoising capabilities of variational auto-encoders (VAEs). Our research uses pattern recognition to mitigate noise inherent to differentially private mechanisms without violating privacy constraints, leading to improved accuracy. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets conclusively demonstrate that this approach significantly surpasses existing benchmark solutions in terms of effectiveness.

In this paper, the (1+1)-dimensional higher-order Broer-Kauf (HBK) system is investigated using the consistent tanh expansion (CTE) technique, demonstrating its solvability under this method. Additionally, exact interaction solutions occurring between various nonlinear excitations, including solitons, rational and periodic waves along with their corresponding images, are explicitly derived.

This study investigates a scheduling scenario aimed at averaging minimal age, subject to simultaneous transmission constraints over unreliable channels where only user fractions are active. Determining the optimal schedule in such environments is widely recognized as a challenging endeavor. Prior works suggest utilizing the Whittle index policy as a computationally simple heuristic to lower system complexity. Despite its implementation convenience, rigorously characterizing the performance and behavior of this specific index-policy has remained notoriously problematic. Building upon intricate mathematical methodologies distinct from previous studies and avoiding arbitrary assumptions, we introduce a robust new analytical approach. We establish the optimality and accuracy of White's index-policy for scenarios with numerous users and specific network architectures. These findings confirm the index-policy for the AOP-minization challenge, boasting analytic assurances in the regime with numerous users and large systems. We conclude this work by presenting simulation results, which substantiated our theoretical analysis, and illustrate how our proposed approach is a robust strategy for large systems.

"Learning through selective omission, which filters out less relevant information, is a ubiquitous and effective strategy in human cognition supported by psychological research. Building on the role this skill plays in helping individuals focus, our work investigates its utility within machine learning. We introduce a new methodological approach known as Learning by Ignoring (LBI)—an automated framework that detects pretraining samples suffering significant domain shifts compared to the target distribution via learning-specific ignore variables, subsequently excluding them. The framework structures optimization across three phases: minimizing loss via ignore-weighted pretraining, finetuning the model, and updating ignore variables based on validation performance. A gradient-based solver is developed to manage these three-staged interactions efficiently. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets confirm the efficacy of LBI."

The solar chromosphere is a dynamic, complicated region where critical physical processes occur on extremely small spatial and temporal scales. Diagnostic spectral lines offer complex data that are difficult to interpret without robust realistic mathematical frameworks. What components are essential for these models to succeed? Magnetic field structure plays the pivotal role here, as easily demonstrated by widespread chromospheric fine strands observable both on the solar disk and at its limb. The numerical simulations outlined in this work reflect current modeling status, illustrating our ability to replicate diverse chromospheric structures and dynamics with accuracy. This release analyzes how varying factors influence model outcomes and outlines a specific approach for developing highly realistic counterparts. When integrated with observational data, these models will provide deeper insight into the mechanisms governing the solar atmosphere.

Wasserstein dictionary learning functions as an unsupervised methodology to discover a set of probability distributions from which observed ones arise as Wassersedstein barycentric combinations. Current approaches in this field aim to find a dictionary that, through barycentric interpolation, possesses enough representational power to reconstruct the observed training set but fail to enforce structure on the associated coefficients. This inadequacy results in dictionaries that offer dense representations of the data, complicating the interpretation of coefficients and often leading to weaker empirical outcomes in subsequent tasks. By drawing from concepts in sparse Euclidean dictionary learning, our proposal introduces a geodesic regularizer tailored to Wasserstein space, encouraging the representation of each data point using only proximal dictionary units. Our analysis demonstrates that this technique fosters sparsity in the Wasserstein space, effectively tackling the issue of non-unique barycentric representations. Additionally, when data originates as Wassersedstein barycented distributions from a fixed probability model, our regularizer aids in the accurate recovery of the generative components even in settings where the unregularized method is ill-posed. Empirical evaluations across synthetic and real datasets confirm that the geometric regularization yields sparser, more interpretable dictionaries in the Wasserstein space, resulting in improved performance in downstream applications.

Probabilistic time-series forecasting supports dependable decision-making in many sectors. Most forecasting tasks involve heterogeneous data comprising multiple structures and modalities; consequently, extracting both knowledge and uncertainty to produce accurate and well-calibrated forecasts poses a significant challenge. Prior research in multi-modal forecasting typically combines representations from different data views through rudimentary methods like summation or concatenation, failing to explicitly characterize uncertainty for each source. We introduce CAMul, a general framework for probabilistic multi-view forecasting that learns representations alongside uncertainties from diverse data inputs. By dynamically integrating knowledge and uncertainty in a context-specific manner—allocating greater weight to useful viewpoints—CAMul constructs a robust and well-calibrated forecast distribution. Evaluated across multiple domains with varying modalities and data sources, CAMul surpasses other leading probabilistic forecasting models, achieving improvements of more than 25% in both accuracy and calibration performance.

This paper investigates harmonic functions associated with general Dirichlet forms. We first examine the implications of Fukushima's ergodic theorem for those harmonics belonging to the $L^p$-domain of the generator. Subsequently, we establish extensions of Yau's and Karp's Liouville theorems to the setting of weakly harmonic functions; specifically, these variants show that weakly harmonic functions obeying particular $L^p$-growth conditions must be constant. As a direct consequence, we derive an integral criterion characterizing recurrence.

The black hole information puzzle originates from conflicting derivations regarding Hawking radiation within the realms of quantum theory and general relativity. While Hawking initially argued that the radiation is purely thermal, causing the system's entropy to increase strictly during evaporation—thereby reinforcing classical expectations—he simultaneously faced contradictions because quantum mechanics dictates reversible time evolution; consequently, quantum formalism necessitates that the Page curve dictates a subsequent decrease in radiation entropy once established by the Page curve. Recent calculations utilizing the replica trick have validated this entropy decline and unveiled a geometric basis in spacetime wormholes traversing replica systems. This investigation analyzes the tension between Hawking's original non- thermalized conclusions and modern quantum information insights, focusing significantly on the quantum de Finetti theorem. This theorem posits the requisite presence of external information ($W$), distinct from the radiation ($R$), which functions effectively as a measurement reference frame; thus, replica trick results yield the conditional entropy $S(R|W)$, contrasting with Hawking's total, unconditional $S(R)$. Because this mutual information ($W$)-conditional entropy constitutes a mathematical ensemble average that acquires practical verification in systems employing multiple identically prepared black holes ($N$)—where, for sufficiently large $N$, the normalized joint entropy $S(R_1 \cdots R_N)/N$ matches the theoretical prediction—the deviation between conditional $S(R|W)$ and unconditional $S(R)$ reveals underlying correlations among black holes. Consequently, spacetime wormholes emerge not merely as mathematical constructs but as a structural representation encoding these correlations. Finally, these findings propose a robust extension of random-unitary models for the large-multiplicity scenarios observed in ensemble averages, underpinned by extensive verificational consistency.

Unsteady pressure-sensitive paint (PSP) data, as an example of time-series measurements, often includes considerable random noise. Therefore, this study proposes a noise-reduction approach merging Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (MSSA)—which employs state-space reconstruction via time-delay embedding—with low-dimensional data representation obtained through Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) projection. The efficacy of this "Projected MSSA" technique is evaluated against Truncated SVD, a widely used denoising method, specifically for processing unsteady PSP data. Results demonstrate that the Projected MSSA outperforms Truncated SVD in attenuating random noise. Furthermore, unlike Truncated SVD, Projected MSSA displays lower sensitivity to the chosen truncation rank. By effectively deriving smooth state-space trajectories directly from noisy inputs, Projected RSSA achieves robust denoising. It is anticipated that this methodology will prove valuable for reducing noise across not just PSP data, but also other forms of high-dimensional time-series.

Heavy particles with masses significantly exceeding the TeV scale cannot currently be accessed through experimental methods. To date, Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) offers the most robust constraints on such particles, particularly restricting the lifetime of those exceeding this mass range to at less than 0.1 second. We demonstrate that the limits regarding both mass and duration derived from the primordial era can be markedly strengthened by future gravitational wave (GW) interferometer technologies, which could detect signals originating from particles with lifetimes as brief as $10^{-16}$ seconds. The fundamental mechanism relies on these particles potentially overwhelming the universe's energy budget, inducing an era of matter domination that precedes BBN due to their subsequent decimation. The deviation of cosmological evolution in this scenario—from the prevailing single-phase of pure radiation—leaves distinct, detectable imprints within stochastic background gravitational waves generated by the primordial epoch. Specifically, we illustrate how identifying GW signatures stemming from extended-duration mechanisms like cosmic strings serves as a distinctive method to constrain fundamental particle physics parameters. By analyzing specific production frameworks within the early universe, these resulting GW spectra enable fresh restrictions on ultraviolet extensions of the Standard Model. We highlight several cases, including supersymmetric models allowing constraints on the mass scales of scalar moduli and gravitinos reaching up to $10^{10} GeV$. Additionally, tighter limits can be established for models involving exclusively gravitational interaction to define reheating temperatures, as well as determining kinetic mixing values for heavy dark photons at sensitivity levels of $10^{-18}$.

When regulated by a limited set of verified validators, Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLTs) need only a subset of the infrastructure typically employed by public blockchains. This paper investigates a method to leverage this environment by integrating a modified Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerant (PBFT) consensus protocol with an updated Flexible FROST scheme to create a proof-of-authority system. This new protocol is implemented within Bitcoin, a platform valued for its reliability, transparency, and activity, effectively supplanting Bitcoin’s traditional Proof-of-Work mechanism with proof-of-stake authority. The resulting hybrid protocol is proposed as a robust, secure base for both digital payment platforms and Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC).

With quantum programming maturing, there is an expanding development of quantum languages and a resulting surge in the need for effective debugging and testing. Although classical bug fixing has progressed significantly, the field lacks comparable research into quantum code. Addressing this gap, our paper offers an extensive analysis of bug fixing specific to quantum programs. We examined and categorized nine empirical cases, collecting 96 documented real-world bugs alongside their fixes across four major quantum languages: Qiskit, Cirq, ProjectQ, and Q#. Notably, our analysis reveals that the majority (storing over 80%) are quantum-unique bugs, signaling an urgent need for further study in this domain. Furthermore, we have extended the catalog of quantum bug patterns, specifically breaking down math-related issues—the most problematic category—to enhance their practical application. Ultimately, these findings define the characteristics of quantum code errors, establishing a foundation for future efforts in quantum verification and debugging.

The outcomes demonstrate an astounding rate increase, specifically approximately a 2.6-fold profit, compared to existing performance metrics, thus providing an efficient signal modulation method by utilizing pattern arrangement.

We introduce a novel, computationally efficient first-order approach to Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML). Our method treats MAML as a bilevel optimization problem, utilizing sign-based stochastic gradient descent (SignSGD) as the lower-level optimizer. This variant is named Sign-MAML. Distinct from traditional first-order MAML (FO-MAML), Sign-MAML lacks the restrictive assumption of ignoring second-order effects during meta-training and is firmly grounded in theoretical justification. Experimentally, Sign-MAML surpasses FO-MAML on diverse few-shot image classification benchmarks, demonstrating a significantly more favorable balance regarding both classification accuracy and computational cost when benchmarked against standard MAML.

Higher-order cumulants in conserved charge distributions serve as critical observables, offering sensitive means to probe fluctuations near the QCD phase transition in heavy-ion collisions. The collection of high-dimensional binary response datasets has grown prevalent, largely driven by advances in sampling protocols such as those used in ecology. While multivariate probit (MVP) models are standard for inferences involving lower dimensions, their application to high-dimensional data poses scalability challenges. These challenges stem from the likelihood function's intractability, specifically the need to compute an integral over a multivariate normal distribution with no closed-form solution, using joint parameter estimation. The prevalence of extensive data has significantly boosted the popularity of data-driven modeling in recent years. Although classical physics-based gray-box models maintain physical integrity, they often struggle with complex identification and scaling, and their predictive precision can be restricted by inadequate representational capacity. Conversely, traditional black-box approaches, now commonly utilizing Neural Networks (NNs), frequently deliver remarkable results on a large scale by extracting statistical correlations from data. However, these models disregard fundamental physical laws, risking severe failures when applied to real-world physical systems. Physically Consistent Neural Networks (PCNNs) emerged to mitigate these challenges by combining neural learning with enforceable physical consistency. This study extends PCNNs to simulate building temperature dynamics, offering a comprehensive evaluation against both classical and black-box methodologies. We developed three unique PCNN variants to demonstrate architectural modularity, also providing a formal proof of their physical consistency. Results from the case study indicate that even with a constrained structure, these models achieve state-of-the-art accuracy, surpassing traditional neural networks that lack physical constraints. The research further highlights how neural networks can produce misleadingly high metrics despite being devoid of domain physics. Despite the computational demands of classic approaches, our findings suggest that PCNNs achieve accuracy gains ranging from 17 to 35 percent relative to alternative physically consistent methods, establishing a pathway toward highly scalable, robust modeling.

In medical image analysis using federated learning, ensuring protocol safety is essential. However, these systems are vulnerable to adversaries attacking either the private data within the federation or the integrity of the models. This paper introduces a complete end-to-end learning architecture designed for forecasting future frames in point cloud sequences. The performance of our network has been evaluated against moving digit instances from MNIT datasets (appearing as MINST and dynamic body simulations of humans, and dynamic body motifs of JPEG). The experimental outcomes indicate that our method yields superior accuracy by outperforming baseline approaches that disregard critical geometry-based feature information.

We examine a spin-1/2 fermion bilayer honeycomb model at half-filling subject to interlayer spin-1/2 local Heisenberg interactions. Via variational Monte Carlo simulations, we observe a direct shift from a Dirac semimetal phase into a symmetric, gapped state identified as symmetric mass generation (SMG) as the Heiseberg coupling increases. This phase transition lacks spontaneous symmetry breaking or topological order and is proposed as an instance of a fermionic deconfined quantum critical point (fDQCP). Our results indicate that at the critical transition point, a fermion bilinear mass in the parton spectrum opens up, yet all symmetry safeguards remain intact due to correlations introduced within the entangling variational wave function. Based on these simulation outputs, we derive a critical exponent $\nu=0.96\pm0.03$ and a fermion scaling dimension $\Delta_c=1.31\pm0.04$ at the SMG threshold, aligning well with (2+1)D, fDQCP theoretical forecasts. Consequently, these findings substantiate the theory of fermion fractionalization occurring at the critical symmetric mass generation point for this matter field transition.

Database transactions offer a critical abstraction, permitting developers to treat blocks of code as isolated executions. {\em Serializability} represents the peak level of consistency, essentially guaranteeing the atomic nature of transactions as if they operated in strictly serial order, similar to sequentially consistent memory. Because achieving strict serializability imposes steep costs system wide—particularly regarding availability—the contemporary approach involves implementing looser guarantees like {\em Snapshot isolation} ($\$S\$-iso). Generally, applying these diminished consistency models to software that mandates serializability leads to correctness violations. Yet, a segment of software remains unperturbed when this consistency level decreases; their validity characteristics enforced by serializability remain true even within weaker consistency environments and without extra explicit synchronization, often described as robust programs.

In general, this work sets forth methods to assess the robustness of code under Snapshot isolation, confirming if a specific program's observable behaviors align with serializability despite execution in a weak database environment. We find this validation issue tractable: it is polynomial-time transformable into determining state reachability in transactional systems utilizing atomic, sequentially consistent shared resources. By converting the robustness check this way, established validation technologies originally intended for strongly consistent contexts can be leveraged instead; notably enabling a proof strategy inspired by Lipton's history conflict theory to certify the robustness of practical applications.

Immersive 3D media represents a growing sector focused on capturing, encoding, and reconstructing the three-dimensional visual aspects of objects and people, finding utility in domains such as gaming, entertainment, distance presentation, and tele-conferencing. This paper introduces a new approach to streaming live 3D interactive media within a serverless environment, specifically proposing a network-centric, adaptive streaming framework. Distinct from traditional 2D video methods, our model relies on centralized production of transcoding profiles. By evaluating the trade-offs between consumer metrics and provisioning expenses while forecasting quality-of-expectations, this framework optimizes outcomes without relying on client-device adaptation mechanisms for quality determination. Furthermore, our analysis highlights why a direct and unrefined application of the serverless concept can lead to inefficiencies specifically when handling various common immersive 3D media scenarios.

Logic-based process calculi, including $\pi$DILL and CP, serve as a framework for deadlock-free concurrent programming but strictly preclude non-determinism and race conditions. HCP constitutes a refined version of CP designed to remediate a primary deficiency: the parallel composition operator intrinsic to the $\pi$-calculus lacks a corresponding rule in linear logic, leaving without equivalent term construction. This paper introduces Non-deterministic HCP (NHCP), which expands HCP through a fresh modeling of non-determinism. Leveraging the principles of bounded linear logic, our methodology establishes a robust typing scheme for standard non-deterministic expressions common in untyped processes. We demonstrate that this expansion is sufficiently expressive to encompass numerous applications of non-determinism found in untyped settings, such as non-deterministic choice, all while maintaining HCP's critical meta-theoretical guarantees, notably freedom from deadlock.

Although nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) is valuable for characterizing local materials properties, it frequently encounters limitations due to low signal-to-noise ratios. Spin squeezed states overcome these constraints by achieving sub-Heisenberg-limits sensitivity along specific spin components, findings now successfully applied to enhance the precision of atomic clocks and elsewhere. Since systems featuring interacting, entangled spins coupled through non-linear dynamics serve as prime platforms for generating squeezing, we propose using a spin-squeezing metric that could function as a probe of emergent quantum-order phenomena. Specifically, we illustrate methods for characterizing an anisotropic electric field gradient through its association with nuclear quadrupole moments, leveraging its influence on spins. Furthermore, while ideal squeezed spin ensembles are in a pure state, methodologies exist to determine the squeezing parameter even for mixed states. Finally, we identify the specific thresholds of temperature and field strengths where maintaining thermal equilibrium is viable to boost NMR resolution and effectively interrogate pertinent anisotropic parameters within the quadrupole Hamiltonian.

Utilizing strong periodic optical driving holds potential for the coherent manipulation of quantum material properties at extremely brief time scales. Recently, techniques capable of significantly transforming electronic and magnetic traits by inducing non-standard band topologies, emergent magnetic coupling, and superconductivity via light have gained traction. In contrast, the methods and potential of engineering optical response on demand in a coherent manner remain poorly understood. We present here an instance of robust coherent manipulation and massive modulation within an optically non-linear material: the van der Waals layered magnetic insulator, magnesium phosphorus trisulfide (MnPS₃). By exciting the system significantly far-off-resonance from its lowest manganese $d$-$d$ electronic transition in MnPS₃, we observed an optically gated on/off switching of the harmonic frequency efficiency (specifically, optical second harmonic generation). This switching occurs with a temporal resolution of 100 femtoseconds and exhibits zero discernible dissipation. At driving electric fields roughly reaching $10^9$ volts/meter, observed contrast between on and off states surpassed a factor of 10—an improvement constrained solely by limitations imposed on the specimen before damage occurs—validated through models grounded in Floquet theory, employing a single-ion formulation of MnPS₃ which simulated both the driving field amplitude and polarization variations accurately. Our strategy may also prove effective for widespread classes of insulators, paving the way for the advent of dynamically tunable nonlinear photonic architectures.

We describe a novel phenomenon analogous to the spin reorientation transition (SRT), occurring at two distinct magnetic fields designated as $B_{SORT1}$ and $B_{SORT2}$. Using a crystal field model approach, we calculated that small Mn$^{3+}$ magnetic clusters within wurtzite GaN—when in their paramagnetic phase—manifest this effect. The resulting data indicates that magnetic anisotropy (MA) undergoes a sign inversion as the magnetic field $B$ increases across $B_{SORT}$ thresholds. However, further examination reveals that the magnetic anisotropy remains constant under high external fields. This behavior, driven by the interplay between the crystalline environment and the spin-orbit interaction ($\lambda \hat{\textbf{S}}\hat{\textbf{L}}$), has been termed the "Spin Orbital Reorientation Transition" (SORT). The specific values for $B_{SORT1}$ and the magnitude of $\lambda$ control these transitions; the former generally correlates with crystal field parameters and the number of ions $N$, while the latter is determined primarily by the strength of $\lambda$. Our explanations are articulated through analyses of spin ($M_S$) and orbital momentum ($M_L$) contributions toward total magnetization ($M$). Similar phenomena may occur in diverse materials provided their systems exhibit positive spin-orbit coupling ($\lambda$), non-quenched ($Non-zero\ L$) orbital angular momentum (L), and uniaxial magnetic anisotropy to occur.

We introduce a technique designed to identify and isolate the static aberrations found in nearly diffraction-limited spectrographs, which are often caused by manufacturing flaws or misalignment. These systems consist of two optical segments separated by a slit or image slicer positioned at an intermediate focus plane. A primary difficulty in this instrument design is distinguishing between errors originating before the slit in the first stage and those occurring after the slit in the second stage; however, our approach successfully resolves this distinction. By separating the measurement of these aberrations, we enable targeted optimization, such as realignments, which subsequently reduces distortions and improves overall optical performance. Our method hinges on fitting computational models to several images of a point source, capturing the effects of controlled displacements of the source (orthogonal to the slit) alongside controlled defocus adjustments of either the detector or the secondary optical stage. Modeling this data allows for the simultaneous extraction of phase errors occurring in both steps. Our significant realization is that analyzing these displaced, out-of-focus images introduces supplementary data points that serve to remove ambiguity between the two optical segments. Simulations provided in this paper confirm the effectiveness of the proposed technique.

This study analyzes how social relationships and structural balance (Heider's balance) evolve in various actor networks under social noise, modeled by temperature. Two lattice configurations are examined: one formed by deleting links from a regular triangular lattice to create a dilated structure, and another by adding links for an enhanced topology. The full spectrum of graph densities within this triangular framework is reviewed, spanning from small clusters isolated into triads to completely connected networks. Results show that when the average node degree closely matches the characteristic value of a standard regular triangular lattice, achieving a balanced state is impossible. Otherwise, the network resides in either a (partially) balanced or unimbalanced state based on temperature. A first-order phase transition into the ordered state is detected exclusively in sufficient high-density networks, whereas less robust lattices—including all those diluted networks—exhibit a continuous crossover. Crucially, this crossover temperature correlates only with system size in density-enhanced networks, whereas in dilated networks, it remains independent of system size and mirrors what is observed for the critical temperature in highly dense enhanced formations.

This paper explores decentralized dynamic multi-agent systems (MAS) designed for resource allocation, where the agents operate under competitive equilibrium conditions to balance supply and demand. The study begins by examining MAS over a finite horizon, where agent utility functions are parameterized to reflect individual needs and shaped via a specific selection of utilities to maintain socially acceptable equilibrium prices; these are bounded by a predetermined affordability threshold proving conceptual solvability for the problem. The authors then transition to quadratic MAS, framing the associated social shaping challenge as a multi-agent linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem, which allows for the derivation of explicit utility sets utilizing dynamic programming and quadratic programming methods, along with a novel algorithm to determine a precise parameter range ensuring compliance with affordability constraints. This paper investigates semi-supervised learning as a strategy to tackle the visual attribute prediction task. Precisely recognizing object attributes is a critical yet demanding aspect for vision algorithms because establishing an unambiguous class hierarchy is difficult. Consequently, datasets inevitably suffer from imbalanced classes and few labeled instances, resulting in sparse annotations and a shortage of reliable data. A logical approach to this issue is leveraging unlabeled imagery to develop effective image representations. Guided by this objective, we introduce the Multi-Teacher-Student (MTSS) framework, drawing from multi-task learning and distillation-based semi-supervised learning principles. The MTSS model applies label embedding to create specialized domain experts known as teacher networks for distinct attributes, while training a universal "student" network to imitate the output distributions these experts uncover. Exresults indicate that this method delivers state-of-the-art performance across several benchmarks for predicting fashion attributes, while also bolstering model robustness and the ability to adapt to unseen and out-of-domain settings.

The proposed method outperforms prior expressive TTS models, such as Tacotron2-GST, demonstrating significant gains in both speech fidelity and expressivity.

Although advancements in automated scientific claim verification have yielded systems approaching human-level accuracy, their efficacy remains unproven within realistic environments involving extensive scientific corpora. Transitioning to open-domain evaluation presents distinct obstacles, most notably the impracticability of fully human annotating all relevant evidence documents. Addressing these limitations, this study introduces SciFact-Open, a novel evaluation dataset containing 500,000 scientific abstracts designed to benchmark verification systems. Utilizing pooling strategies from information retrieval, evidence for these claims was gathered by aggregating and labeling the top outputs generated by four state-of-the-art verification models to overcome full-annotation bottlenecks. Results show that models optimized for smaller datasets struggle to transpose to SciFact-Open, suffering performance degradation of at least 15 in F1 scores. Furthermore, examining the evidentiary content uncovered critical patterns indicative of real-world deployment issues, such as instances supporting only partial or specific aspects of a claim associated with scientific topics. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/dwadden/scifact-open.

Although techniques like model visualizations serve as windows into the inner workings of neural networks and reveal details missing from outputs, doubts persist regarding whether these explanations truly align with actual model behavior. Specifically, can they detect pathological states like shape bias or backdoors? To address this evaluation gap, anomalies are defined as deviations from a reference set of standard models; we then examine whether explanatory techniques differentiate between these anomalies and normal operation. Our findings indicate that while current tools can identify pronounced irregularities such as adversarial training or shape bias, they often miss more nuanced deviations arising from incomplete training data. Additionally, they generally fail to isolate specific anomalous inputs, such as the triggers embedded for backdoors. Ultimately, our analysis exposes new limitations in current explanatory transparency, emphasizing the critical need for improved methodologies without, however, altering the message that such tools can indeed fail to interpret maliciously or irrationally trained systems when scrutinizing specific input behaviors. They highlight current limitations suggesting there remains work before we can fully understand a model during the analysis phase itself. Ultimately they find transparency still suffers from gaps that impede reliable detection when certain failure indicators do match expectations but lack sufficient support elsewhere within their overall output structure.

Secondary currents emerge within turbulent, wall-bounded flows subjected to longitudinal topographic variations like ridges aligned with the flow direction. This phenomenon forms streamwise-aligned vortical structures referred to as "Prandtl's vortices of the second kind." Extensive prior literature indicates that specific characteristics of these turbulent structures, such as vortex strength and internal organization, vary alongside different ridge architectures. This study employs the linearised RANS framework by Zampino (2022) to examine how ridge geometry influences current formation, comparing outcomes for symmetric configurations containing rectangular, elliptical, and triangular ridges. Results indicate that analogous flow organizations exist across these distinct geometric profiles, particularly for isolated and small-size ridges; in such scenarios, the intensity of secondary flows remains dependent on ridge geometry primarily when scaled with ridge height. Detailed exploration of complex geometries reveals that while scaling behavior consistently predicts secondary flow generation and shape-specific flow organization for trapezoidal ridges, it is observed that non-scaling conditions can trigger the emergence of tertiary flows; here is how this phenomenon occurs.

This work introduces NEREL, a Russian corpus designed for named entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction. We introduce a supervised learning methodology for training regularizers designed to enforce sparsity during the denoising of signals and images. While sparsity-promoting regularization is essential for modern signal reconstruction tasks, its associated operators have historically been either heuristic-based learned without ground truth data. Recent triumphs of supervised techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks, in image reconstruction motivate the creation of such optimized regularizers. Consequently, we adopt a variational framework that utilizes a parametric, sparsity-inducing regularizer, where its parameters are adjusted to minimize mean squared error on training datasets comprising clean images and their corresponding noisy measurements. Training this model necessitates addressing complex bilevel optimization; we derive a specific gradient for the loss function based on the analytical solution to the denoising task alongside a gradient descent procedure. Empirical evaluations on 1D structured signals and natural photographs demonstrate that our learned operator significantly outperforms established methods, including standard regularization techniques like Total Variation, DCT-sparsity methods, and unsupervised dictionary learning, as well as collaborative filtering approaches in denoising tasks. Additionally, despite focusing on denoising in our presentation of the approach and study methodology in the abstract for signal/image reconstruction, there is an implication that applications in wide-ranging contexts with general classes involving inverse problems and multiple measurement models.

Contextual bandits serve as a cornerstone in industrial personalization architectures. These frameworks are engineered to derive a treatment assignment policy that adapts to the varying treatment effects observed alongside user-specific contextual features. Although personalized user engagement fosters experiences reflecting individual preferences, there is significant value in shared community interactions that align users with the current zeitgeist via network effects; such collective benefits elapse beyond standard regret metrics used in bandit evaluation. To reconcile this tension, we introduce a novel algorithm that orchestrates a tradeoff between high-fidelity personalization and increased cross-user treatment uniformity. Specifically, our hybrid model interpolates selectively between contextual and non-contextual multi-armed bandits, relying solely on environmental cues when their marginal utility is demonstrable beyond random assignment. Beyond enhancing the user balance between novelty and conformity, simplifying treatment mechanisms through selective context reliance has shown potential to accelerate learning convergence. We validate our hybrid strategy through a binary classification experiment using public datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to the prior approach.

The velocity distribution function serves as a statistical framework bridging particle dynamics and macroscopic properties within many-body systems. Laser-induced fluorescence (LIF) spectroscopy is often employed to measure local velocity distribution functions in spatially non-uniform plasmas, though determining an explicit analytic form for these distributions can be elusive under the complexities of non-equilibrium conditions. This study introduces a novel strategy to identifying appropriate analytic forms of such functions using Bayesian statistics. We developed a framework for the Bayesian inference of ion velocity distribution functions and applied it to locally acquired LIF spectra across multiple positions in a linear magnetized plasma. The results verify spatial inhomogeneity by evaluating the validity of each candidate form for the local velocity distribution function. This methodology demonstrates broad utility in experimentally establishing velocity distribution functions in both plasmas and fluids.

Process mining allows business leaders to identify and examine real-world workflows by leveraging event data commonly present in IT systems, offering deep insights supported by these highly detailed logs. However, this granular information frequently incorporates sensitive or private details, making privacy concerns a critical focus that has prompted the development of new solution methods. To ensure these methods remain accessible, specialized tools are required to combine these techniques and steer practitioners toward the right strategies based on their specific scenarios. We introduce here, a Python-driven infrastructure that integrates current privacy and confidentiality protection approaches within process mining. The tool offers an intuitive web interface for publishing private-preserving data, conducting risk assessments, and performing data utility evaluations. It also enables various anonymization operations designed to bolster data safety, supports both standard and non-standard event datasets, and includes functionality to store and manage privacy metadata for monitoring the effects applied to the logs.

Furthermore, it delineates the discrepancies between guided and free-space atom interferometry responses in environments subjected to extraneous forces. Finally, both theoretical and technical hurdles essential for advancing this emerging quantum technology ecosystem are addressed as part of the transition to a realized platform.
