We conduct a leading-order perturbative QCD study of the gravitational form factors (GFFs) for nucleons under a large momentum transfer framework. This analysis yields explicit factorization equations expressed through twist-3 and twist-4 light-cone distribution amplitudes. The resulting power behaviors of these GFFs are estimated based on the leading-order computations. Additionally, using established model assumptions, numerical evaluations of quark and gluon contributions across various GFFs are reported. The paper also includes perturbative determinations of the pion and proton scalar form factors, $ \langle P'|F^2| P\rangle $, at high momentum transfers.

Gourdeau et al. (2019) previously established that distributional assumptions are required for the robust learnability of concept classes when optimizing exact-in-the-ball robust risk with random example access. In contrast, we investigate scenarios where learners possess local queries. We present the first distribution-free algorithms capable of robust empirical risk minimization (ERM) and robust ERM for local equivalence queries. We demonstrate that while the learning threshold remains constant under the uniform distribution regardless of the query radius, distribution-free robust learning remains unachievable if a query radius is chosen to exceed the adversary's parameter. In our experiments, we found that the query radius is bounded, which allowed us to avoid the requirement for distribution-free robustness when the query radius is less constrained. We also note that the query radius is bounded, which implies a fixed learning threshold under the uniform distribution for local equivalence queries. Finally, we address two classes where we derive robust ERM guarantees. We also discuss robust ERM for half-spaces, which allow the learning threshold of conjunctions to remain unchanged, and provide algorithms that learn with margin for two important cases involving local equivalence queries. We then consider the query radius to determine if robust ERM is feasible under the assumption of random example access; our results confirm that a distribution free-learning model with queries can circumnavigate previous constraints to learn any robust ERM for local equivalence queries. We then examine the case of half-spaces, which includes two important subsets. Finally, we explore the possibility of learning robust ERM for local equivalence queries in distribution free-learning models.

Recent Super-Resolution (SR) advancements have primarily been validated on standard imagery—such as faces, landscapes, and objects—rather than the Earth Observation (EO) domain. This study evaluates leading SR algorithms on specific EO datasets and employs both Full-Reference and No-Reference Image Quality Assessment (IQA) metrics. Additionally, we introduce QMRNet, a Novel Quality Metric Regression Network capable of performing as a No-Reference predictor by learning any desired imaging characteristic (whether resolution-based or specific distortions), while also enabling hyperparameter optimization of SR algorithms to meet target quality metrics. QMRNet is a component of the IQUAQFLOW framework, a broader solution for assessing EO data, detecting and classifying objects, and implementing image compression with a user-defined ground sampling. In our experiments applying and evaluating QMRNet against features including GSD-related properties, noise (N-R), edge sharpness (S-N-R), blur (B-S-N-R), GSD retrieval, and edge sharpness (S-N-R), we achieved a mean absolute difference less 1 pixel in predicted features and recall values exceeding 90% across 15 unique dataset. Overall results show the robustness and practicality of CAR and MSRN architectures alongside the prospective role of the QNRNet method as a loss function to better guide SR. Additionally, we demonstrate the generalization capabilities and modularity of the QNRNet method which could be utilized across various imaging domains given its lightweight architecture and scalable processing flow."

For many decades, researchers have dedicated significant resources to enhancing linear and nonlinear mixing models in order to solve hyperspectral unmixing; however, these models are still restricted in handling concurrent spectral variabilities and identifying physically accurate endmembers due to inadequate data reconstruction and fitting, alongside their high susceptibility to such variability. Drawing from the robust learning capacities of deep learning, this study presents the Endmember-Guided Unmixing Network (EGU-Net), a comprehensive approach for hyperspectral unmixing designed with a specific focus on the nature of endmembers derived from hyperspectral data. Unlike standard autoencoders, EGU-Net operates as a two-stream Siamese architecture. It employs a secondary network trained on purely or near-pure endmembers to calibrate parameters within an unmixing network via shared weights, thereby imposing spectrally meaningful restrictions such as physical abundance constraints (e.g., non-negativity and fractional sum-to-one) for improved accuracy and interpretability. Moreover, beyond addressing pixel-level unmixing, the robust framework facilitates spatial-spectral unmixing through convexolutional operators for spatial feature modeling. Experiments on multiple datasets with ground-truth abundance maps validate that the proposed EGU-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art unmixing techniques; the source code will be made public via GitHub.

Cluster galaxies currently demonstrate markedly reduced star formation compared to those in sparse environments (the field), suggesting they may have been more star-formative earlier in cosmic history. Drawing from the Horizon-AGN large-scale cosmological hydrodynamic simulation, we interpret the star formation history (SFH) of cluster and group galaxies. Our analysis reveals a universal trend for massive galaxies—where the star formation activity declines with relatively short e-folding timescales regardless of location—a phenomenon known as mass quenching. Conversely, low-mass stars show significant reliance on environmental conditions. Within massive halos characteristic of clusters prolonged tenure amplifies the reduction in star formation for low-mass galaxies through "environmental quenching," a finding aligned with theoretical predictions on ram pressure stripping. We define a "transition epoch" representing the time when cluster systems fell behind field ones in star formation activity, a timing that fluctuates based on both stellar mass and the host halo's mass. Observations indicate that while low-mass galaxies in massive clusters began this transition approximately 7.6 Gyr ago in the past, that shift was more recent (roughly 5.2 Gyr ago) for massive galaxies located within less formidable clusters. Ultimately, these results enable a description of cluster galaxy SFH that considers the ratio of cluster halo mass to stellar mass.

We study norm maps within algebraic even K-theory concerning finite extensions of number fields, primarily establishing their surjectivity in most scenarios. Where these maps fail to be surjective, we provide a specific condition to determine if an element in the even K-group of the base field is the norm of an element from the even K-group of an extended field; notably, this criterion depends exclusively on the field's real prime locations.

**Optimizing relational databases involves solving the multi-objective problem, where several objective functions must be optimized at once, requiring specialized techniques. This paper surveys existing approaches for resolving these issues within relational database contexts. Specifically, the research investigates two primary queries—the Top-k query selects k optimal results for a given set, while the skyline query takes advantage to return all top trade-offs. In addition, the performance of Flexible skyline query is discussed; it is a new approach engineered to enhance and overcome the limitations found earlier algorithms. For all presented strategies we delve on key characteristics of the algorithm's underlying and evaluate their relative pros and cons.**

This study investigates the relationship between kinematics and wake properties within a tandem two-foil system with chord-length separations ranging from four to nine and various interfoil phases by integrating experimental and simulation data. An extensive wake analysis was conducted, where turbulous kinetic energy was quantized along with mean wake velocity. Using this energy assessment, trailing foil efficiency was refined to encompass not just energy from shed coherent leading edge vortices (LEVs) but also contributions from mean wake flows. A predictive wake model utilizing mean wake velocity identified two distinct regimes based on the efficiency profiles and primary LEV strength of the trailing foil by classifying the two-foil system. This regime classification serves as a pragmatic strategy to narrow configuration parameters and enhance harvesting efficiency.

Leveraging IBM's cloud quantum processor, we demonstrated the efficacy of LEOs across three potential subspace scenarios within two and three-qubit Hilbert spaces, observing significant suppression of leakage currents in both.

This work investigates the hop-constrained shortest path enumeration (HcPE) problem: for a given undirected or undirected-like graph $G$, two distinct vertices labeled $s$ and $t,$ and an integer constraint $k$, the task involves retrieving every simple path from $s$ to $t$ where the number, edge, or max distance of the steps (the hop limit) is less than the specified $k$. Recently, most current high-end methods in real-world implementation suffer from slow running speeds, which come as a direct performance cost to using them when dealing too many edges in path search due. These methods cannot handle or meet up with current online system and application demands over real-world time constraints. In response to these problems, we propose an enhanced and efficient approach of an indexing-based method developed for the highly optimized and scalable HcPE problem: `PathEnum`. As part of this, for each search request, we initially construct a lightweight index to limit the number, size, extent or scale and scope complexity of which the edge nodes will play in computation and traversal processes, while also providing high-efficiency indices with two distinct approaches: The first utilizes Depth-first traversal; The latter makes effective usage of SQL or Relational Database Join operations in terms of efficient performance. In essence, we use specific technologies to ensure fast processing speeds via a lightweight index to limit the number, size, extent or scale and scope complexity of which the edge nodes will play in computation and traversal processes. If required we even provide additional query optimization features that utilize the mentioned cost models to adjust and balance trade-off the cost of searching for optimal performance. Graph data comes in various structures. Directed graphs indicate link orientation, whereas signed graphs distinguish between positive and negative relationships; consequently, signed directed graphs merge both aspects but remain under-explored due to the relative infancy of their convolutional processing methods. Most current graph convolution models cater specifically to either undirected or unsigned structures. This study investigates a spectral graph convolution network tailored for signed directed graphs. We introduce a new Hermitian complex adjacency matrix capable of encoding network information, where link directions and signs alongside connectivity are represented through phases and magnitudes, respectively. Furthermore, we derive a magnetic Laplacian based on this Hermitian framework, proving it possesses positive semi-definite properties. Our proposed Signed Directed Graph Convolution Network (SD-GCN) targets tasks such as link sign and ultimately represents the inaugural application of spectral convolution to graphs with signs. Uniquely, the SD-GCN offers broad applicability, handling undirected, directed, and signed networks alike, whereas prior convolutions were often constrained to single data type. Validated on four real-world datasets, the model surpasses all state-of-the-art convolutional methods specifically in determining link signs.

This study establishes a partial ordering, termed $P_{\lambda}(2)$, on the set of maximal chains for any finite bounded poset $P$ admitting a CL-labeling $\lambda$; we refer to this construction as the maximal chain descent order generated by $\lambda$ . For illustration, if $P$ represents the Boolean lattice equipped with its standard EL-labeling, the resulting $P_{\lambda}(2)$ serves as a representation isomorphism of the weak order of type $A$ . We closely analyze additional instances, noting that the max-min EL-labeling of the partition lattice corresponds to the maximal chain descent order, which is isomorphs to the structure on a specific class of labeled trees. Furthermore, linear extension EL-labelings of certain finite distributive lattices produce maximal chain descent orders isomorphs to partial orders acting on standard Young tableaux . Cache side-channel vulnerabilities pose significant risks to software security and privacy, particularly affecting cryptosystems. To address this, we introduce CaType, an advanced static analysis tool based on refinement types designed to detect side channels in cryptographic software. Compared to existing solutions, CaType offers three key advancements: First, for the past time, we leverage refined types to analyze cache side channels in x86 assembly code, enabling bit-level tracking, differentiation between variable impacts, precise typing inferences, and enhanced scalability; Second, CaType is the inaugural static analyzer to explicitly account for blinding defenses within crypto libraries; and Third, regarding implementation, we mitigate false positives by modeling cache layouts of potentially vulnerable control-flow instructions rather than direct cache states. Empirical evaluation of real-world cryptographic applications—includingRSA, ElGamal, and (EC)DSA from OpenSSL and Libgcrypt—shows that CaType not only identifies all known flaws but also uncovers previously unknown vulnerabilities and corrects errors in prior tools. Performance-wise, CaType analyzes these libraries 16 times faster than CacheD and 131 times faster than CacheS, validating its high precision, efficiency, and scalability in detecting security deficiencies.

Federated Learning (FL) represents a form of distributed learning wherein edge devices cooperatively train models in place of their data, keeping it shared neither between users nor with a centralized controller. This study introduces two adapted iterations of the widely recognized FedAvg approach tailored for multi-model federated settings, complete with formal convergence proofings. Additionally, we demonstrate that, compared to individually training each of the individual models in an analogous amount time computing, simultaneous utilization can lead toward significantly enhanced performance outcomes. This paper explores the determination of when a specified stochastic process yields a sampled Brownian filtration. By applying Frank H. Clarke contraction criteria to a construction based on the quasi-invariance of a sampled Wiener measure via a specific criterion, authors derive rather broad sufficient conditions rooted in the analytical properties of a sample Brownian motion. Furthermore, these findings establish sufficient conditions for the existence of solutions within a class, potentially including non-Markovian stochastic differential equations influenced by this sampled Brownian motion, extending notably to continuous time models when the sampling frame coincides with the unit interval.

Within a variational framework accounting for non-equilibrium screening, this study examines the stationary regime of a spin-Hall device. By minimizing the system's dissipated power and adhering to global constraints imposed by an electric generator as well as charge conservation and spin-flip relaxation, analytical formulas are derived for spin-accumulation, pure spin-current components along both longitudinal and transverse axes. These expressions are calculated under two distinct conditions: negligible and dominant spin-flip scattering. Given the short Debye-Fermi screening length, the results demonstrate that spin-accumulation varies linearly with position ($y$) and the generator-induced electric field while exhibiting a temperature dependence of $1/T$ specifically within non-degenerate conducting systems.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are now integral to many safety-critical computer vision tasks, such as automated driving and human-robot collaboration. To ensure these systems remain functional in real-world settings, it is essential to defend against hardware memory faults. Drawing on the known effectiveness of activation clipping, this study establishes a preliminary safety argument for convolutional classifier by showing that range supervision acts as a robust detector and countermeasure against specific bit-flip faults when utilizing eight-exponent floating-point representations. Additionally, we investigate new non-uniform range restriction strategies that substantially lower the likelihood of silent data corruption and uncorrectable errors. As a proof of practical application, our model demonstrates improved vehicle recognition in an end-to-end traffic classification scenario using the MIOVision dataset with ResNet-50. The quantitative results presented here can serve as a foundation for developing more sophisticated CNN safety justifications.

We present a spline-based approach adapted for real-time visual-inertial odometry (VIO) in a continuous-time framework. Here, poses are modeled using cubic splines, with their temporal derivatives synthesizing linear acceleration and angular velocity. These values are matched against IMU measurements to facilitate optimal state estimation. Boundary conditions imposed on the splines generate constraints linking camera poses and inertial measurements. Consequently, VIO is structured as a constrained, non-eucliden optimization problem. Representing poses continuously in time allows for effectively addressing complex challenges such as rolling shutter effects and unsynchronized sensors; furthermore, this modeling ensures high-accuracy results while being computationally efficient enough for real-time execution, as demonstrated by our experiments across two open-source benchmarks.

This study investigates the application of nonlinear ordinary differential equations and optimal control theory in the development of epidemiological models for Ebola virus disease (EVD). Specifically, we conduct an optimal control analysis on both SIR and SEIR frameworks for ESD dissemination. The controls employed for the analysis include vaccination, treatment, and educational campaigns as time-dependent variables, utilizing standard indirect methods involving the Pontryagin maximum principle and Hamiltonian functionality. This approach enables the construction of adjoint equations and optimality sytems which are then solved using a fourth-order Runge Kutta method within a backward-forward sweep algorithm. Numerical results indicate that the effective introduction of educational programs, combined with targeted treatments for infected individuals and prevention efforts through vaccination to susceptibles play crucial role which can successfully lower disease burden and help reduce Ebola's spread.

The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting significantly influences a nation's economy by shaping corporate transactions and interactions. Briefly, netting offers an alternative to standard inter-company payment processes; it functions as an agreement where mutual debts are offset and the payment obligations of two or more parties are converted into direct settlements based on their respective balances. This paper introduces a suite of graph algorithms designed to provide optimal netting solutions on the scale of a countrywide economy, calculating results with computational efficiency. Tested using invoice data from the Romanian Ministry of Economy, our findings demonstrate that classic graph algorithms remain effective in addressing critical issues of great importance.

Software Defined Networking (SDN) represents an emerging network architecture currently garnering significant interest due to its distinctive capabilities. A variety of recent studies have focused on verifying the correctness of SDN data plane configurations. Fundamentally, SDN switches direct traffic based on established flow rules; these rules collectively map out implemented paths. This paper introduces a new preventive method for validating that no misconfigurations—such as infinite loops—will occur given specific requested path requirements. We explain the necessity of this verification: during the synthesis of data paths, unintentional and undesirable configurations (including loops) outside the specified request may emerge. Moreover, we demonstrate scenarios where satisfying a specific requested set of paths necessitates the accidental creation of undesirable behaviors, implying that only a superset can practically be implemented. Accordingly, we provide verification technology to detect these potential misconfigurations, analyze their methodological complexity—and notably, our polynomial complexity suggests practical relevance—and outline a technique for path debugging and repair. This ensures that any corrected set of paths does not induce unwanted behaviors, provided such adherence is physically feasible.

We introduce a Bayesian graph neural network (BGNN) designed to derive weak lensing convergence ($\kappa$) from galactic photometric data specific to a certain line of sight. This approach holds significant relevance for strong graphical time delay cosmography (TDC), a field where accurate determination of the external "convergence" ($\kappa_{\rm ext}$) stemming from the ambient line-of-sight lens population and large structures is crucial for high-precision $H_0$ estimation. Utilizing large-scale simulations initially at $\kappa$ resolutions near $\sim 1'$, we incorporate galaxy-scale perturbations of $\sim 1''$ to generate random sightlines as training inputs. Performance is subsequently assessed against varying levels of test-set distribution overlap. Across evaluation sets of 1,000 distinct sightlines, individually inferred BGNN $\kappa$ posteriors feed into a hierarchical Bayesian framework to constrain governing population hyperparameters; this workflow recovers population-mean $\kappa$ precisely without systematic error in well-training-covered regions, introducing a forecastable contribution to the total $H_0$ uncertainty well below 1%. Within training-dataset sparse regime limits that mimic distribution tails signal loss, BGNN outperforms traditional approaches reliant solely on galaxy count matching by effectively leveraging the complete information of every line-of-sight, thereby overcoming statistical variance constraints typical of the simpler methods found elsewhere. This hierarchical, BGNN-based pipeline offers the potential for enhanced precision characterizing $\kappa_{\rm ext}$ for Time-Demand Cosmography (TDC). The code implementing this methodology is freely distributed through the Python library "Node to Joy."

Ultimately, our results indicate that electroweak multiplet dark matter is efficiently trapped within neutron stars. Visual object tracking serves as a vital component in numerous video-based applications. Although significant advancements have been made in this field, current deep learning-based trackers frequently struggle with targets undergoing substantial appearance variations. A primary reason is that these models generally lack online updating mechanisms or the ability to update individual model sub-branches, limiting their adaptability. Consequently, efficient updating techniques are essential; yet, existing meta-updater approaches, which operate directly within the parameter space, are prone to over-fitting or collapse in long sequences. To overcome these challenges, this work introduces a context-aware tracking model that optimizes within the representation space instead. By jointly meta-updating both model branches and leveraging historical sequence information, the proposed approach avoids over-fitting. Specifically, recognizing that the local-focused localization features (involing target details) and global-focused box-estimation features (involving the target's surroundings) complement each other effectively, the method designs two key components: (1) a context-aggregation module that fuses historical frame features to refine these local/global inputs, and (2) two parallel context-aware modules for the branches individually to learn affinity vectors. Furthermore, the framework employs a specialized meta-learning algorithm to ensure fast and robust updates even with minimal training samples, ultimately enhancing the base tracker in just 5 minutes of training. To evaluate the tracking performance, the method achieves an EAO (Expected Average Overlap) of 4.84 on the TEMoT-21 benchmark set.

This work analyzes the jet substructure and transverse momentum ($p_{\rm{T}}$) composition in centrality-specific Pb-Pb collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 2.76 TeV. Using a tracking resolution parameter ($R$) of 0.3, charged jets located at midrapidity were identified within the angular range $|\eta|_\text{ch-jet} < 0.6$, covering transverse momenta from 30 to 120 GeV/$c$. Measurements of jet-hadron correlations are performed in relative pseudorapidity-azimuth plane ($\Delta \varphi$, $\Delta \eta$) to examine how particles surround the jet axis across several associated particle $p_{\rm{T},\text{assoc}}$ intervals spanning 1 to 20 GeV/$c$. Results in Pb-Pb environments are juxtaposed against $pp$ reference distributions derived from embedded PYTHIA simulations. For associated high-$p_{\rm{T}}$ particles (where $4 < p_{\rm{T},\text{assoc}} < 20$ GeV/$c$), Pb-Pb data show a 10% to 30% suppression compared to these references, a reduction that varies with collision centrality. Compared to PYTHIA predictions, the particle distribution radially relative to the jet axis exhibits a moderate modification in Pb-Pb collisions; the surrounding activity is somewhat more tightly collimated at high $p_{\rm{T}$, while lower $p_{\rm{T}$, associated particles display a tendency to broaden. Represented for the first time down to jet $p_{\rm{T},\text{ch-jet}}$ of 30 GeV/$c$, these findings align with earlier jet-hadron measurements from the CMS Collaboration and jet shape data from the ALICE Collaboration measured at higher momenta. Consequently, they further substantiate the current understanding regarding parton energy loss within the hadronic medium.

Spin waves emerge as highly promising, charge-free information conduits for achieving future energy-efficient post-CMOS electronics, distinguished by their versatile excitation methods, diverse interactions, and readiness for nonlinear dynamics. Despite significant progress in rapidly advancing magnetic research, theoretical frameworks for capturing multi-modal nonlinear behaviors within nanostructured propagating waves remain undeveloped; addressing these challenges is a critical objective of ongoing study. This work undertakes a rigorous theoretical exploration of the dynamic coupling between an incoming spin-wave beam and the localized edge-bound waves in a thin ferromagnetic film. Our findings demonstrate the emergence of an inelastically scattered beam, which appears alongside a specularly reflected component that experiences frequency shifts characterized by increases and decreases relative to the edge mode. Crucially, we identify a robust correlation between the edge-mode's frequency and the angle of the scattered beam, leading to the formulation of an effective signal demultiplexing technique for magnons confined to propagation limits at the edge. Since magnetostatic dynamic interactions drive this process and resemble ubiquitous phenomena across spin-wave systems, these mechanisms suggest broader applicability and promise future implementations in various magnetic device architectures.

Quantum machine learning approaches suggest potential performance gains for machine learning tasks. This paper presents two novel quantum methodologies for neural networks. The primary method is a quantum orthogonal neural network that utilizes quantum pyramidal circuits as foundational blocks to execute matrix multiplication within an orthogonal module [1]; we further propose training algorithms suited for both classical and quantum hardware, with asymptotic scaling advantages over prior techniques. Additionally, the second method involves a quantum-coupling scheme for performing inner-product estimations during both the inference and training phases of classical neural architectures, thereby leveraging quantum capabilities to augment traditional CNN frameworks. Finally [3], we demonstrate various experiments across medical imaging datasets by deploying both existing and simulated quantum hardware to juxtaposes the capabilities of hybrid systems against classical baselines; empirical data suggests that across multiple quantum frameworks, the results converge with classical neural architectures, thereby validating the feasibility and utility [9547] using hardware advancements.

Complex phenomena, often visualized through network landmarks, involve interactions among various agents that evolve simple local rules into emergent, nonlinear behaviors. Although recent studies connect network structures to their dynamic underlying processes, recognizing these spontaneous dynamic remains an enduring challenge. In this work, we present a straightforward, data-defined framework utilizing operator-theorem methods to both detect and regulate stochastic nonlinear dynamics on vast networks. Our method necessitates zero prior knowledge of the network's topology, determining the essential mechanics solely from pairs of sequential states. By leveraging the Koopman operator, this process maps high-dimensional patterns onto a low-dimensional space where evolution is effectively linear, enabling precise identification. Furthermore, employing this global linear model, we apply Model Predictive Control (MPC)—typically difficult on massive networks—to resolve critical control issues. Our solution transforms the inherent non-convex optimization problems into highly manageable, convex frameworks with a significantly reduced variable count.

We report a multi-instrument study of a C1.3-class solar flare occurring within active region NOAA 12734 on 8 March 2019. Data were collected from the SBO satellite's AIA and HMI instruments as well as the Udaipur-CALLISTO solar radio spectrograph. Despite its low intensity, the event displayed classic long-duration characteristics, including extended flare arcs, expansive two-ribbon structures, and paired coronal dimmings. Emerged in a coronal sigmoid, the activity featured two distinct phases of energy release that can be traced spatially and temporally. We infer a massive rising flux rope with footpoints anchoring the eastern and western margins of the sigmoid based on the location of twin dimming regions. During the second phase of flaring, the Udaipur-CALLISTO observations identified a broadband (approximately 50–180 MHz) and approximately stationary plasma emission lasting nearly 7 minutes. This emission pattern is comparable to a type IV burst. Preceding this type IV emission by five minutes was a type III radio burst spanning decametre and hectometre bands, initiated at roughly 2.5 MHz. Combined analysis incorporating Non-Linear Force Free Field (NLFFF) coronal models, multi-wavelength observations, and magnetic decay index evaluations indicates that the flux rope rose through the plasma akin to a zipper and from the west toward the east due to an overlying asymmetrical field. This directional ejection by the flux rope helps explain observed phenomena like an apparent west-to-east migration of flare ribbons, the movement and twisting of post-flare loops relative to the polarity inversion line (PIL), suggesting that the site of magnetic reconnection propagated laterally as the eruption continued.

We present Region-Based Explanations (RbX), a new, model-agnostic framework that creates local interpretations for scalar outputs from black-box prediction systems using only query access. RbX operates through a greedy algorithm designed to construct a convex polytope that approximates the feature space neighborhood where predictions remain similar to those at a designated target. Notably, the user defines this region based the scale of the predictions themselves rather than individual feature scales. The spatial geometry of the resulting polytope—specifically, the magnitude of the coordinate shift required to exit it—measures the local sensitivity of the outputs to each feature. Subsequently standardizing these "escape distances" allows for ranking features by their local significance. RbX inherently satisfies a "sparsity axiom," ensuring features absent from a prediction model receive zero importance. Additionally, both empirical analyses on real datasets and synthetic experiments confirm that compared to current methods, RbX can identify locally relevant features with greater ease.

Performance verification indicates that this proposed methodology significantly improves over current best-practical ordinal regression techniques, with notably enhanced classification accuracy for indeterminate, or "unrelated," and benign cases.

Recent advancements have seen a trend toward pre-training increasingly large language models to test the capabilities of deep learning, yet doing so from scratch consumes massive computational resources and ignores existing models, leading to unnecessary inefficiency. Extensive experiments across prominent pre-trained language models, including BERT and GPT variants like BERT\_BASE and GCP\_BASE, confirm that: (1) the approach slashes training costs compared to baselines such as learning from scratch, StackBERT, and MSLT; (2) the solution is versatile enough to apply across various pre-trained model types. Interaction frames serve as essential models for clarifying and interpreting experimental designs in magnetic resonance. They frequently simplify spin Hamiltonians by removing their dominant components—such as subtracting the Zeeman Hamiltonian within the standard rotating frame to isolate spin dynamics details, or excluding the radiofrequency (rf) Hamiltonian to evaluate the efficiency of decoupling or recoupling strategies. Transitioning into an interaction frame may also transform time-dependent Hamiltonians into time-independent ones, as happens to the rf-field Hamiltonian within the conventional rotating frame. Removing the primary energy term enhances comprehension of spin behavior, while it can additionally minimize energy differences, thereby accelerating the convergence of perturbative methods like average Hamiltonian and Floquet theory, or series expansions. Although multiple interaction frames often lack obvious initial solutions and vary in convenience relative to the problem context, this section uses selective dipolar recoupling as an example to examine the comparisons and trade-offs among options. Suitable frameworks consistently encompass the entire radiofrequency Hamiltonian and may incorporate chemical shifts and effective fields over the duration of a pulse sequence, or exclude the effective components altogether depending on the choice.

The Gauss-Markov theorem establishes that the weighted least squares estimator serves as a linear minimum variance unbiased estimator (LMVUE) for linear models. This paper proposes an extension of that result to non-linear frameworks by integrating depth constraints into machine learning. While traditional methods derive non-linear minimum variance unbiased estimators using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)—often requiring resource-intensive real-time computations—deep learning offers non-linear estimation with invariant computational loads. Although learning-based approaches excel on training data in the average sense, they can introduce substantial bias across other parameters. To mitigate this, we introduce a bias constraint within the objective function, creating a "Bias Constrained Estimator" (BCE) that guarantees asymptotic minimum variance unbiased properties matching the behavior and Cramér-Rao limits of classical estimators. Beyond signal-to-noise ratio and covariance estimation applications, BCE addresses distributed settings involving multiple averaged measurements of the unknown, such as in sensor networks or test-time augmentations, where our method ensures asymptotic consistency and improves overall precision under these conditions as shown.

This study introduces a wavelet denoising approach tailored to signals embedded in Gaussian noise when information regarding the signal's $L^2$-energy is known. Peer code review is recognized and utilized extensively in both open source and commercial software development, although existing research indicates that reviewers often submit a substantial portion of non-productive feedback. Regrettably, there currently are no tools available to offer automatic assistance in enhancing such inefficient comments. This paper presents a comparative analysis contrasting text-based features and reviewer seniority against useful versus unhelpful feedback. Building on these insights, we propose RevHelper, a prediction model designed to assist developers in enhancing review quality by forecasting comment utility upon submission. Analysis of a study set consisting of 1,116 comments revealed that high-utility feedback shares greater lexical overlap with the specific code changes introduced and highlights salient elements, primarily submitted by more experienced reviewers. Further testing on 1,482 additional comments showed that the RevHelper model achieved 66% accuracy in predicting comment usefulness. A comparative case study utilizing three baseline model variations supports these preliminary findings and highlights the practical potential of the proposed approach.

For a typical two-level atom interacting within the quantized field of a resonant cavity, thermal effects at finite temperatures result in the excitation of cavity modes, which masks the measurement of quantum atom-light interactions. In this work, we demonstrate that a hybrid setup combining a superconducting cavity with a quantum multi-level (complex) atom allows for several key observations; even under finite temperature conditions at strong couplings, we are able to retrieve the system toward a specific equilibrium and exhibit interactions permitting extraction (via feedback loops) of excess quantum entangled photon from the coupled system into the ground-state, thus isolating the vacuum field quantum fluctuations even at 4~K for realistic experimental conditions; also demonstrated is that cooling in more traditional schemes works better when fewer photons, thus ensuring that such theoretical work remains experimentally feasible for application in quantum control via coherent mixing in cavity qubit arrays or other protocols in quantum circuits.

This study centers on the algebraic framework governing complexity and algorithm development for the Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP). We consolidate, refine, and extend elements of three distinct methodologies applied to finite template-based CSP research: the absorption theory utilized in "JACM"14 to identify constraints solvable via local techniques, and the independent theories proposed by Bulatov and in "ZOCS"17/JACM"20, both pivotal to deriving the CSP Dichotomy Theorem. Our primary contribution presents an elementary result concerning primitive positive definability, from which key starting points in Bulatov's and Zhuk's arguments emerge as corollaries. Secondly, we launch an exploratory analysis of minimal Taylor algebras. This extensive class of algebras is uniquely structured, allowing the Dichotomy Theorem to be verified solely on this subset while exhibiting notable stability; notably, concepts divergent in general theory align within this specific class. We posit that the theoretical groundwork laid here will ultimately yield a simpler, more intuitive derivation of the Dichotomy Theorem through an algorithm with reduced complexity, and further advance complexity investigations in other CSP-associated domains.

Traditional stochastic Galerkin applications to two-dimensional shallow water models equipped with random inputs risk sacrificing the equations' hyperbolic properties, potentially altering the fundamental physics. Our study proposes a revised theoretical framework where hyperbolicity remains intact through the rigorous selection of polynomial chaos expansions for the nonlinear components of the shallow water system. We establish a sufficient guarantee for maintaining this hyperbolicity, contingent solely on enforcing finitely many positivity constraints on stochastic water depths across specific parameter-space quadrature nodes. Guided by this analytical approach, we formulate a robust central-upwind discretization. Numerical experiments validating this enhanced central-upwind strategy reveal both its high accuracy and stability in addressing demanding test problems, proving its effectiveness where prior stochastic Galerkin systems often fail or exhibit numerical issues.

To enhance user comfort and mitigate Virtual Reality (VR) sickness in immersive telepresence settings, we introduce a rotation "unwinding" technique. Immediating telepresence involves streaming audio-visual feed from a 360\textdegree~camera on a remote robot to a head-mounted display worn by the user, allowing them to appear present and interact remotely as they observe by moving their heads or communicate with those nearby. While traditional VR often forces the user's screen to rotate with the robot's movement, our approach decouples the camera's orientation changes from the user's fixed horizon in local reality, allowing viewpoint adjustments solely through body rotation within the user's actual room. Since conflicting motion between the eyes and inner ear—a primary cause of VR discomfort—can cause sickness, we experiment that aligning these stimuli via user-directed turning will improve safety. Validating this on a virtual mobile robot with 38 users in a user study (N=41) (comparing unwinding rotations to real-time camera rotation tracking). Data illustrates users favored unwinding rotations and reported lower sickness. Noteworthy further contributions are observations linking to path integration strategies, viewing tendencies, and qualitative findings regarding simulated speeds, distances.

Few-shot learning addresses the significant challenge of gaining knowledge from limited labeled examples while achieving generalization across new tasks by drawing upon prior information from related domains, effectively facilitating rapid adaptation despite scarce data. In our work, we introduce MetaKernel, a meta-learning approach employing random Fourier features as dynamic kernels. By adopting the random feature basis as a latent variable and utilizing variational inference, our method data-driven learns these features while leveraging shared insights from related tasks modeled in meta-learning. This integration achieves context-specific posterior inference through long-short term memory components. Furthermore, conditional normalizing flows utilizing coupling layers generate a more expressive posterior distribution over random Fourier basis vectors, yielding highly representative kernels that leverage shared information for enhanced model expressiveness. These kernels improve both the accuracy of individual images and overall learning performance in few-shot scenarios. Comprehensive evaluations on few-shot image classification and regression confirm via ablation studies that all proposed modules contribute to robust performance while achieving results on fourteen benchmark datasets with at least parity and often exceeding existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Importantly, we achieved notable improvements measured objectively by the PESQ scores reaching 0.5 levels on the datasets derived from noisy environments where prior approaches fell short; furthermore subjective feedback from listeners revealed our methods improved clarity further by approximately one point of MOS scores compared directly against those same chaotic originals.

Fluctuation-dissipation relations (FDRs) and time-reversal symmetry (TRS), which serve as fundamental pillars of statistical mechanics, both fail in generic driven-dissipative systems, leading to non-equilibrium steady states far from thermal equilibrium. While driven-dissipative models of the Ising type were presumed to show standard effective thermal criticality near phase transitions, we demonstrate that FDR and TS are in fact macroscopically broken, either at or near these critical points. This observation was verified by examining various observables—including both time-even and odd operators relative to TRS—specifically looking for their correlation and overlap with the order operator. Surprisingly, despite these symmetries being inherently broken, we show a generalized version of the FDR and a specific form of modified TRS nonetheless take hold; however, these modifications result in profound implications for response and correlation functions and alter Onsager reciprocity relations significantly. Finally, we establish that at the critical point, time-reversal symmetry breaks completely, even when considering the limit of weak dissipation.

Advancements in sequencing landscapes are generating fresh prospects for genomic investigations. This study introduces a straightforward protocol for inferring HLA profiles directly from Whole Genome Shotgun (WGS) long-read sequences by bypassing intermediate files to pipe alignments straight into HLAminer. Ultimately, these multiple streams of information are combined dynamically to produce final probabilistic outputs. Large-scale experiments using a prominent public benchmark have established that the proposed method is both effective and efficient, yielding strong quantitative and qualitative results. This research opens avenues toward quantitatively analyzing metallic quantum phenomena, such as nontrivial superconducting phases.

Regression models for continuous outcomes frequently necessitate a transformation of the response variable; this is traditionally determined either beforehand by the analyst or inferred within a specific parametric framework. In this work, we establish the asymptotic characteristics of CPMs when implemented with censored outcome data at the extremes. We demonstrate the uniform convergence of both the predicted transformation functions and estimated regression parameters within the valid, unobstructed intervals and outline their concurrent limiting distribution. Simulation evidence indicates that when only minor portions of the data undergo censoring, the inferences from CPMs on such censored datasets closely mirror those obtained on complete data. Additionally, we apply and contrast CPMs in the context of a real-world reanalysis of HIV patient data.

If the snippet scores highly, it remains unavailable for comment generation, and the IR-based method is invoked instead of being replaced solely by neural-generated output.

To mitigate this uncertainty, we introduce a novel map constructed using a Gaussian distribution assumption. This approach converts the binary nature of object detection into continuous probability estimates, enabling probabilistic data association between artificial features and semantic information. In our method, update iterations assign weights proportionally, granting higher confidence scores to more reliable detections and lowering weights at detection boundaries. These mechanisms reduce uncertainty, thereby minimizing its detrimental impact on nonlinear optimization. Empirical evaluation using the TUM RGB-D dataset indicates that our system improves upon ORB-SLAM2 accuracy in indoor settings by approximately 15%, successfully validating the approach in dynamic environments.

A primary hurdle in creating computationally viable, high-precision predictive models for complex turbulent flows involving numerous species is the prohibitive computational expense of solving individual transport equations for every single species. To address this, the paper introduces an on-the-fly reduced order framework designed to efficiently handle reactive transport and its associated passive scalar equations. Our method achieves dimensionality reduction by decomposing species profiles into three specific, time-varying elements: (i) a collection of spatial basis vectors orthogonal to each other; (ii) a low-rank structure representing the instantaneous correlation matrix among species pairs; and (iii) a low-dimensional, time-evolving coordinate system defined by orthogonal species components. Unlike data-driven methods such as proper orthogonal decomposition (PCA), which rely on solving and discretizing the full dimensional species field to extract modes, our approach directly derives the necessary low-order modes by projecting and solving them within the species convection-diffusion-reaction transport operators themselves. We then formulate evolution laws for these three components using the variational optimality conditions of the transport problem itself. Because all components evolve over time, the resulting basis can automatically and dynamically adjust to non-steady changes in the chemical state. We present numerical experiments demonstrating effective reduced order representation for both passive diffusion and complex chemical kinetics using this strategy.

This manuscript introduces the exponential transient excision algorithm (ETEA). Designed for biomedical time series analysis—including *in vivo* neural recordings and electrocorticography (ECoG)—this approach targets measurement artifacts characterized by piecewise exponential transients. The efficacy of this algorithm is demonstrated through results derived from synthetic signals as well as actual EEG and ECoG datasets.

Entropy measures serve as nonlinear tools for gauging time series complexity, with permutation entropy widely utilized for its robust and rapid calculation capabilities. To analyze multichannel datasets requiring examination beyond individual series, specialized multivariate entropy methods are necessary. In response, this work introduces $MPE_G$, a multivariate permutation entropy derived from graph theory.

The $MPE_G$ algorithm processes multivariate inputs through two primary steps. First, it constructs a Cartesian product graph $G$ combining two components ($G_1$ and $G_2$), where $G_1$ retains temporal sequences from each signal and $G_2$ captures inter-channel relationships. Second, it treats the multivariate signal as discrete samples on this underlying graph and applies graph-specific permutations. By design, this graph-based framework offers the versatility to handle varied data configurations and cross-channel dependencies while addressing the constraints of existing multivariate permutation entropy techniques.

Gathering ample labeled data to develop human activity recognition (HAR) models is costly and time-intensive. Furthermore, training solely on existing data often results in models biased toward the training distribution, causing them to fail miserably on unseen distributions. While transfer learning and domain adaptation aim to resolve these issues, they typically require unlabeled target domain access that may be unfeasible in practice. Addressing this lack of focus on generalizability for unseen target scenarios in HAR, this work introduces SDMix, a novel approach for effective cross-domain HAR. Our method integrates semantic-aware Mixup, designed to handle domain-induced semantic inconsistencies by respecting activity semantics, alongside a large margin loss. This loss enhances discrimination among Mixup samples to mitigate misclassification from potentially erroneous virtual labels. Extensive experiments across five public benchmarks show that SDMix significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 6% in both cross-person and multi-dataset settings, as well as tasks with different sensor locations.

Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS) exhibits exceptional potential for resolving computationally challenging problems in graph theory, such as clique detection on intricate graphs. Since structural drug design methods like molecular docking can be modeled as finding maximum cliques, GBS presents an avenue for enhancement. Executing this quantum-based molecular docking requires fully programmable, large-scale quantum hardware, a milestone not yet achieved by even the latest GBS systems. In response, we developed a universal, programmable, and highly scalable time-bin GBS photonic processor featuring adjustable squeezing parameters and the ability to execute arbitrary interference operations via an interferometer. This processor successfully solved a 32-node clique-finding problem, achieving a detection probability for the maximum weighted clique roughly double that of classical sampling. Furthermore, we instantiated a functional, yet quantum-powered platform for molecular docking that successfully simulated binding for two clinically significant proteins aimed at combating cancer, nervous system conditions like Alzheimer's, or inflammatory states such as ischaemia. This work marks a breakthrough in GBS circuit design thanks to our distinctive universal software, pushing the technology closer to practical implementation.

This paper explores anomaly clustering, which organizes anomalies of similar types together. In contrast to standard anomaly detection—whose goal is solely to segregate anomalies from normal data—our approach is distinct because it must handle subtle, localized anomalous patterns, unlike object-centric image clustering where anomalies tend to be more pronounced. To achieve this, we propose a simple yet robust clustering framework that utilizes patch-based pre-trained deep embeddings combined with existing out-of-box clustering techniques. Since images are represented as a collection (or "bag") of embeddings, we introduced a distance metric defined by the Euclidean separation between these weighted average vectors, where the assigned weights reflect the importance of specific patch instances and emphasize problematic regions. These weights are determined either in an unsupervised manner or semi-supervised when access to labeled normal samples is possible. Rigorous experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework and its novel distance metric against various multi-instance and depth-based clustering methods. On benchmark objects and texture categories from the dataset [sic], our model achieved normalized mutual information scores of 0.451 (objects and textiles, respectively); the addition of a limited amount of normal supervision data boosted these results slightly. Complex networks often originate in the real world and are typically modeled using graphs; yet, these structural ablations usually assume that relationships are strictly binary (connecting only pairs of nodes). Because many scenarios—including social interactions, peer-to-peer systems, and academic co-authorship—feature more intricate dynamics, the hypergraph model offers a superior and natural alternative. As a generalization of standard graphs, a hypergraph allows a single edge (hyperedge) to link any number of vertices, thereby enabling accurate representations of multi-relational, many-to-many networks and facilitating the discovery of subtle dependencies. Managing these structures requires specialized software libraries capable of handling tasks ranging from basic traversal and algorithm implementation to complex computations, such as community detection, as well as deriving significant network metrics. This paper introduces SimpleHypergraphs.jl, a novel software library implemented in the Julia programming language engineered for high-performance computing. Specifically, the work unveils the library along with two new analysis techniques: s-betweenness centrality and an adapted label propagation algorithm, alongside visualization capabilities for hypergraph representation, creating intuitive interface tools. These claims of utility are validated through two practical case investigations utilizing Yelp's 2019 Challenge, dataset, and collaborative networks inspired by the "Game of Thrones" television franchise. Ultimately, the empirical outcomes affirm that hypergraph-based methodologies deliver more nuanced insights into collective behavior than conventional methods that focus solely on the adjacency.

Achieving sample-efficiency in reinforcement learning has long been a challenge, particularly within scenes characterized by high complexity and numerous components. Objects from new, known sets can utilize pre-learnt, context-specific models for their respective state dynamics and any rewards associated with moving them. Recent research highlights the constraints of exclusive text pretraining. Our findings reveal that color distributions recovered by language models align more closely with the distorted distributions prevalent in natural language data than with ground-truth values, thereby confirming that reporting bias inherently hampers text-only learning. Federated learning (FL) offers a decentralized approach for hospitals to train collaborative models while retaining private patient data locally. Specifically in an FL setting, hospitals send model training outputs instead of data samples to a central coordinator. Nevertheless, sharing model parameters or gradients can inadvertently reveal the privacy of the underlying training data and individual patients. To counter this, our implementation employs secure multiparty computation (SMC) within an FL framework designed for data protection. The system first groups hospitals into clusters; after each hospital performs localized model training, its weights are fragmented among other members within the cluster. This distribution prevents any single entity from isolating the weights of any other hospital in its cluster. All hospitals then transmit these aggregated shard weights to the central server. The server subsequently calculates the average model by summing the contributions without ever observing individual hospital weights. Our experiments were evaluated using data from the The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) benchmark repository. When comparing our proposed framework against baseline methods of differential privacy and standard Federated Averaging (Federated Averaging protocol), findings suggest that the new strategy achieves superior accuracy compared to the differential privacy approach. Furthermore, our method offers security guarantees against privacy leakage, though it does involve higher communication overhead.

An analytical framework governing domain wall structures in ultrathin films is detailed, specifically for materials exhibiting a perpendicular easy magnetic axis, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction at interfaces (DMI), and external arbitrary in-plane fields. The problem is resolved through the efficient minimization of a single-variable analytical function. When compared against micromagnetic simulations using parameters typical of current devices, the analytical model demonstrates excellent agreement, allowing discrepancies from simpler existing models—specifically those permitting variation only in the wall moment's planar direction—to be examined; in these gaps, the presented approach either identifies deviations or offers necessary corrections. Crucially, this method enables precise calculation, depending on the in-plane field's magnitude and orientation, of key properties such as domain width and tension, which regulate domain wall mobility in these types of ultrathin layers.

The superconductor-insulator transition (SIT) observed in thin-film disordered superconductors stands as a classic example of a quantum phase transition. More than three decades since its discovery, its fundamental nature remains a subject of intense discussion, particularly regarding the unique characteristics of the insulating side. A key area of concern involves the current-voltage ($I$-V) relationship, which displays distinctive anomalies: (1) conductance changing suddenly by multiple orders of magnitude as voltage increases, (2) hysteretic phenomena, and (3) frequent minor current jumps alongside the primary transition. Although various models have been previously proposed to address experimental data, no model has yet fully accounted for these complex behaviors. A prevalent method involves treating the disordered system as a two-dimensional grid of conductive islands where charge carriers tunnel adjacent to each other, typically predicated on the assumptions of rapid relaxation, ensuring the system remains in electrostatic and thermal equilibrium. This equilibrium framework successfully describes certain measurements, including the transition itself, but fails to generate hysteretic features in the predicted $I$-V curves. In contrast, our study proposes a revised approach that integrates finite relaxation time into an array model, demonstrating that under slow relaxation conditions, such a model can accurately reproduce both hysteresis and the multiple discrete jumps found in the $I$-V curves. Based on these findings, we posit that analogous behavior ought to be observed in two-dimensional arrays of normal (non-superconducting) materials—a view further bolstered by existing experimental records. Furthermore, our investigation evaluates the influence of various model parameters, identifies the relevant time scale domains for this system, and aligns our simulations with selected empirical data.

The article introduces a methodology for probabilistically forecasting the trajectories of Vulnerable Road Users (VRUs) that factors in historical movements and environmental context. The individual's past motion is modeled through 3D pose data representing body posture and articulation, while the environment is captured using semantic maps detailing infrastructure like sidewalks and street layouts along with dynamic obstacles. Trajectory predictions are computed as arbitrary discrete probability distributions over spatial grids, assessed based on reliability, sharpness, and localization accuracy. In addition to comparing our method—specifically examining its benefits and limitations when using poses versus Gaussian distributions—we analyzed the influence of both 3D pose data and environmental maps. This analysis utilized a spatial label smoothing technique to ensure forecast consistency. Ultimately 3D pose data provided a clear benefit to the forecasts. Semantic maps allowed probability distributions to be tailored to the specific scene, but at the studied prediction horizon (2.52 seconds), the historical path of the VRU proved more significant. All evaluations were performed on an inner-city traffic dataset collected from a research vehicle, which the authors are releasing publicly.

The origins of millisecond-duration transients, known as fast radio bursts (FRBs), are still not understood, partly because their sources might vary. Some FB Rs are documented as repeat events, while others are not. However, insufficient observation windows and inadequate telescopic sensitivity may cause some periodic bursts to be mistakenly identified as non-repeatable. Therefore, precisely categorizing bursts as either repeaters or non-repeatable sources is crucial to resolving their origins. Using unsupervised learning and avoiding costly monitoring sessions, this study employs Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) to develop a recognition method for recurring FRBs with a distinct objective: to demonstrate UMAP's ability to classify repeaters without prior data on their repetition rates, assess the hypothesis that known non-repeater populations contain hidden repeaters, and identify repeater candidates—without monitoring—that are not currently monitored, providing an updated dataset for these sources. By applying this approach to data from the CHIME/FRB telescope, the researchers achieved a 95% completion rate in detecting repeating sources. Using this unsupervised method, 188 candidates were pinpointed among 474 FRBs originally tagged as non-repeatable, establishing a foundation for future FRB classification based on single-time observations.

Topological photonics has garnered considerable research interest due to its ability to introduce novel principles for controlling light. Optical materials classify their band topology according to the Berry phase associated with Bloch states. Despite this, explicit standards for empirically detecting topological phase transitions in this context remain largely scarce in current photophysical studies. Notably, far-field polarizations of radiating Bloch states define radiation topology via Stokes phases. Although both band and radiation topologies originate from the band structures of Bloch states, they typically appear to evolve largely independently. Our findings demonstrate that radiation topology offers a viable method for investigating phase transitions in band topology. Supported by theoretical designs, experimental validation, and photonic crystals exhibiting quantum spin Hall effects, the research confirms this intrinsic connection. Specifically, as the band topology shifts from trivial to non-trivial, the topological charge of the radiation topology vortex transitions between values such as +1 to -2 or vice versa. Consequently, these observations establish radiation topology as a novel criterion for monitoring changes in fine-band topology. Beyond deepening our conceptual grasp of both topological forms, these mechanisms suggest innovative methods for manipulating both nearby and distant fields of light.

This connection facilitates an interpolation formula for the weighted $q$-Genocchi numbers and polynomials. Furthermore, we derive the Multiplication Theorem and Witt-type formulas for modified $q$-Genocchi objects, offering deeper insights into the utility of such $q$-deformations for traditional $q$-Genocchi terms. The newly introduced weighted generating function exhibits several noteworthy properties detailed herein.

A novel multi-layer numerical architecture, extending the single-layer Saint-Venant system to include non-hydrostatic variations of the Navier-Stokes equations, is employed to characterize breaking wave field statistics. Within this physical space ensemble, phase-resolved surface waves—evolving without explicit surface overturning—are simulated while capturing significant non-linear events such as wave breaking. Breaking front kinematics, specifically their velocity and propagation, are extracted from freely evolving fields generated via typical wind-wave spectral initial conditions. We report the distribution denoted by $\Lambda(c)$, which represents breaking front lengths (per unit area moving at speeds between $c$ and $c + dc$) in line with Phillips 1985 across diverse conditions. Notably, a $\Lambda(c) \propto c^{-6}$ scaling emerges naturally for sufficiently steep fields, even in the absence of explicit wind forcing. Furthermore, a $\Lambda(c)$ scaling dependent only on the mean square wave slope and peak phase speed effectively models the distribution. These simulated breaking rates align closely with observational field measurements and accord with prior empirical models. Consequently, this approach facilitates the direct modeling of the turbulent upper ocean, realistically coupling wave breaking dynamics—such as Langmuir turbulence—with other sub-mesoscale processes.

This article introduces *"The Universe in Words,"* a collection of video descriptions of iconic Messier catalogue objects designed for blind and partially sighted viewers. In addition to fostering inclusivity and enhancing the audience's deeper comprehension of celestial visuals for everyone, inclusive formats like these significantly transmit information more effectively to diverse groups. Furthermore, series can augment on-site events and complement alternative resources, such as sonifications or tactile models.

The recent proliferation and increasing sophistication of AI models have generated significant demands on computational resources. While performance gains are achieved through more powerful accelerators and large clusters, scaling up prediction accuracy yields a steep energy cost, prompting concerns about the environmental impact of AI at scale. Energy efficiency is therefore a critical consideration for both developers and infrastructure managers. Since energy usage varies based on hardware and implementation models, accurately measuring power draw across diverse compute nodes is essential for optimizing algorithms and designing next-generation clusters. In response, we measured power consumption for two typical deep learning tasks across various compute architectures. Our findings reveal that using runtime alone to estimate energy usage is inaccurate; rather, the specific composition of the compute node must be accounted for. Additionally, ignoring accelerator hardware during energy calculations on mixed-type nodes leads to exaggerated inefficiency metrics. Finally, it is crucial to separate the energy footprint of training versus inference. While GPU-based training outperforms other node types in both speed and efficiency, inference runs efficiently on CPU nodes. Conversely, integrating these energy metrics into the supercomputer's user interface makes this data immediately accessible, facilitates the application to future workloads, and enhances overall user awareness of energy usage.

Beyond indirect linking via cavity mediation, these emitters in our Tavis-Cummings framework also interact through direct dipole-dipole interactions (DDI). Applying the mean-field and low-exitation approximations, we concentrate on how DDI influences CPA feasibility when accounting for decoherence factors like emitter spontaneous emission and photonic leakage from cavity boundaries. Additionally, using an analysis of dressed states, we explore the physical principles governing permitted polariton transitions within the Jaynes-Tavis-Cummings energy ladder. A primary finding is that in the strong-coupling regime of cavity QED, significant dipole interactions combined with detuned emitters and resonators enable CPA at two laser frequencies adjustable via inter-atomic spacing, an outcome impossible with a solitary detector even with detunings applied. Spectral land cover segmentation presents a complex challenge that has garnered substantial interest in remote sensing. Despite extensive efforts toward diverse methods, the majority remain dependent on supervised strategies, whereas unsupervised Subspace Clustering (SSC) solutions are popular due to their robust performance. However, SSC algorithms are computationally intensive for large hyperspectral datasets, and because they often disregard spatial information, their discriminative capacity and resulting spatial homogeneity suffer. To solve these dual challenges, this study introduces a rapid method that first identifies a representative subset of pixels within each neighborhood to derive sparse coefficients, followed by spatial filtering to ensure pixel connectivity and fast spectral clustering for the final segmentation. Moreover, the proposed algorithm reduces computational requirements by up to three orders of magnitude compared to standard SSC on datasets exceeding 20,000 spectral pixels.

The goal involves maximizing the achievable system rate by concurrently tuning PS fractions at each receiver, Active Transmit Beamforming (ATB) at the access point, and Passive Reflective Beamforming (PRB) at the IRS, subject to constraints regarding the maximum AP transmission power, phase shifts for every IRS element, individual energy harvesting minima at each PS receiver, and feasible PS ratio domains. Manual inspection and classification of hands-foot X-rays to evaluate joint degeneration in Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) are labor-intensive and depend on trained specialists whose subjective judgments often result in inconsistent agreement. Notably, the inclusion of attention weights offers inherent explainability for the model's predictions, mitigating the typical "black box" opacity of deep learning systems. Implemented during the RA2 Dream Challenge organized by the Rayo Institute Laboratory (DAIMLab)/Dream Challenges, this method advanced in this competition, ultimately claiming 4th place in joint-level and narrowing score prediction tasks.

Within databases, a frequent task is to identify which pairs or k-tuples occur often together. Specifically, a challenge is generating a memory-efficient sketch of the data that flags which k-tuples seem in a significant fraction (exceeding $\epsilon$) of database rows. The description of a molecule's response to UV/Vis electromagnetic radiation is critical and relies heavily on analyzing the molecules' spectroscopic features. While CNN-based holistic methods with margin loss have traditionally led face recognition research, this study diverges from that framework in two key ways. (2018) in unforced contexts, while kNN and in iterative, Deep Neural Network training produce a broad global nonlinear estimation capability, where DNN iteration serves as the primary method. Results demonstrate the substantial outperforming capability: although performance between kNN and DNN remains similar for purely dynamic periodities under actuations, the DNN proves notably more effective in chaotic flow conditions. We further thoroughly compare each method regarding prediction accuracy, complexity, and computational expense, confirming the advantages offered. We argue for extend the application to closed-loop plant applications and for flow control plants in subsequent applications.

Although cryptocurrencies have seen an astonishingly high adoption rate in the last decade, the detection of fraudulent activities within this sector remains severely under-research. Among these illicit acts, "pump and dump" schemes represent some of the most prevalent methods. While some prior studies have examined analogous scams in the stock market, their applicability to the crypto realm is significantly limited by the lack of labeled historical financial data for equities combined with volatility patterns unique to cryptocurrencies that differ from traditional markets. The progress within machine learning and artificial intelligence has accelerated the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles (AVs) on public highways. In rate-distortion optimization, encoder parameters are set by optimizing for high visual quality under a fixed bitrate constraint. Monte Carlo methods are indispensable in particle physics, serving as a bridge between pertative calculations/phenomenological models and the mapping from theoretical predictions to comprehensive detector simulations, especially for high-energy collisions. This work examines general forms based on Braginskii's classic fluid framework (*Rev. of Plasma Phys.*, 1965) by utilizing Grad's moment method alongside the Landau collisional operator. We analyze a 21-moment model, analogous to the Braginskii formulation for multi-species plasmas involving arbitrary mass and temperature variations, which tracks the full evolution of fluid moments; in addition, we explore an alternative 22-moment model. The 21-moment approach captures two "heat flux" vectors (representing third- and fifth-order moments) and two "viscosity" tensors (representing second- and fourth-order moments). Braginskii's model emerges as a specific instance applicable to single ion-electron systems under similar temperature conditions and coupled assumptions where de-coupled approximations are made for viscosity and heat flux alongside the hydrostatic limit. We derive Braginskii's model and included higher-order moments entirely through analytical means, ensuring detailed equations and exact numerical values are provided. In generalized settings, this approach greatly simplifies the computation of transport coefficients and facilitates adaptation to legacy numerical codes, which can be sensitive to whether Hermite or direct fluid moments are employed. We emphasize that coefficients for Braginskii's model diverged in weak-collision limits precisely due to the hydrostatic approximation, and demonstrate in our 21-moment analysis how, in fact, heat fluxes and viscosities remain interconnected despite the hydrostatic assumptions, and moreover how 22-moment scalar contractions of the fourth-order moment reshape the plasma rate of energy exchange. In addition, we offer detailed supplements to guide derivations of Braginskii's model using the Grad moment method for multi-fluid systems, ensuring we can provide specific details for those familiar enough in this domain. Additionally, the appendices serve effectively as supplementary instructional materials. (These supplementary appendices also provide a useful roadmap for practitioners applying the Grad moment approach, ensuring we complete the hydrostatic limit's analysis as intended in this work).

Humans naturally solve tasks flexibly by diversifying their strategies, whether in overall trajectory planning or individual steps, which allows them to readily adapt to and generalize across changing environments. To enable generalization to unseen tasks, we match concise geometric descriptors instead of full trajectory distributions, as these definitions transfer effectively to new task configurations. We experimentally verified this approach using varied robot tasks informed by versatile human examples, comparing it against imitation learning techniques in both trajectory and state-action paradigms. Results demonstrate that employing geometric descriptors significantly improves adaptation to new tasks, and that their combination with the distribution matching objective is essential for successfully modeling and reproducing flexible behavior.
